blocks.h: CRUEL SUN, THE WATER SAID
Roya Publication No. 110
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Lahaina sits on the dry side of Maui, between a green mountain and a blue sea. Long ago it was called Lele, and it was so full of running water that the whalers called it the Venice of the Pacific. Then the sugar planters turned the streams away to their fields. The streams stopped running. The king’s pond was filled in and a ballpark was built on top of it. When the sugar left, the old cane fields above the town filled up with tall dry grass, and nobody cut it.

Kanoe cleans hotel rooms at a resort up the coast. She lives in her grandfather’s plantation house above Front Street with her mother, Tūtū, who has never in seventy-nine years gone into the sea past her knees, and her son Keola, eight, who backflips off the harbor wall every afternoon.

Wes is a high-school swim coach from Ohio. He has come to Lahaina with his son Theo, nine, and with the ashes of his wife in a bag in his backpack, to give her to the sea where they were married. He has taught a thousand children to swim. He cannot teach his own son, who has been afraid of deep water since his mother got sick.
It is the first week of August 2023. A hurricane is passing far to the south. The weather service has raised a red flag. The wind is coming.
And in the gaps between the chapters, something older than the island has started to talk. It is very patient, and it is trying to be gentle, and it is speaking to someone.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book is fiction wrapped around something that happened.

On the morning of August 8, 2023, broken power lines in a high wind set fire to dry grass beside Lahainaluna Road, above the town of Lahaina on Maui. Firefighters put the fire out, and it was declared contained. That afternoon it came back to life in the same place and the wind drove it through the town. It killed one hundred and two people, most of them older people who could not run. It destroyed more than two thousand buildings and left something like ten thousand people with nowhere to live. Some of the people who survived it did so in the sea, behind the seawall on Front Street, for nine hours, with the town burning above them.

I have tried to keep the order of events, the weather and the broad shape of what went wrong faithful to the public record and to what survivors have said: the hurricane to the south and the high pressure to the north, the red flag warning, the power that was not turned off, the fire that was declared out, the sirens that were never sounded, the phones that did not work, the roads blocked by fallen poles and live wires, the hydrants that went dry, the request for stream water that waited on a desk, the people in the water, the surfers who paddled in through the reef in the dark for the children, the list of the missing, the hotels, the texts offering cash for burned land, and the tourists who came back while the search went on. Because this is a story and not a report, I have kept the numbers loose and the times approximate. Some things in the book, like the reports Wes reads at three in the morning, came out over the following year.

Everyone in this book is invented: Kanoe, Tūtū, Keola, Wes, Theo, Claire, Bully, the woman who sang on the hill. The few moments in the water that echo what real survivors described are told without names. Officials appear only by their titles, the Mayor and the Governor, and what they do here is only what was publicly reported. No company is named.

The suspicions in this book belong to its characters and to the water. The observations underneath them are real. I have tried to set the plausible ones beside the absurd ones, with enough of the facts that the reader can weigh them, and then to step back. The official investigations ruled the fire accidental. That answer and the questions around it can both be true.

The nānā honua, the angel’s trumpet, is a real plant, poisonous in every part, and it does grow in Lahaina yards; it is not from Hawaiʻi, and it is not sacred. I have left Hawaiian gods and sacred beings out of this book on purpose. They are not mine to use. The one thing I have bent is the water’s voice, and what Wes hears with his ears under. Everything else was lying in plain sight.

Hawaiian words in this book are written with the marks the language uses, the ʻokina (a small mark for a catch in the voice, as in Mokuʻula) and the kahakō (a line over a vowel that makes it long, as in Tūtū). The narrator from Ohio writes Hawaii the way he always has.
This book is for the people of Lahaina, whose town it is, and for the ones who are still on the list.
Chew Z
I. CRUEL SUN
1. The Water Was Here First Kanoe

My name is Kanoe [kah-NOH-eh]. It means the mist, the soft rain that hangs on the mountain in the morning and never quite reaches the town. My mother picked it. She said she wanted me to remember what we were missing.
That’s a Lahaina [lah-HY-nah] joke. You have to be from here to find it funny, and even then you don’t laugh, you just kind of breathe out through your nose.
Let me tell you where we lived, so you can see it, because it isn’t there anymore and somebody has to carry it.

Maui [MOW-ee] is an island shaped like a person bent over, head and body, two mountains joined by a low neck of land. The small mountain is on the west, and we call it Mauna Kahālāwai [MOW-nah kah-HAH-lah-WHY], the mountain where the waters meet. It is old and green and folded like a cloth somebody dropped, all sharp ridges and deep valleys, and the clouds sit on top of it nearly every day of the year. Up there it rains like it means it. Up there the moss is so thick on the rocks you can push your whole hand into it to the wrist. Down here, on the dry side, on the strip of flat land between the mountain and the sea, is Lahaina. Down here it hardly rains at all.

The old people say the name comes from a chief who was walking here in a drought a long time ago and said, lā hainā [LAH hy-NAH], cruel sun. Tourists like that story. They buy it on T-shirts. What they don’t buy is the other half: that before it was Lahaina, this place was called Lele [LEH-leh], and Lele was not dry at all. Lele was green. Lele was so full of water they called it, later, when the ships came, the Venice of the Pacific.
Here is how that worked, and it is the most important thing I will ever tell you, so I’m going to say it simple.

The rain falls on the mountain. The rain runs down the valleys in streams, and the streams run all the way to the sea. Our people, a long time ago, cut the land into slices that followed the water. Each slice was called an ahupuaʻa [ah-hoo-poo-AH-ah]. Picture a piece of pie with the point up on the mountain and the wide end in the ocean. Every family in that slice had a little of everything: forest at the top for wood and birds, the stream in the middle for taro [TAH-roh] fields (taro is a root we grow in flooded ponds and pound into food), the beach and the reef at the bottom for fish. Nobody owned the water. The water belonged to everybody in the slice, and everybody in the slice belonged to the water. You took what you needed and you let the rest run down to your neighbor, because your neighbor was your cousin and your cousin was going to feed you fish next week.

In our language the word for fresh water is wai [WHY]. The word for wealth is waiwai [why-WHY]. Water, water. You don’t have to speak Hawaiian to understand what our ancestors were telling you with that. If you have water, you are rich. If somebody takes your water, they have taken everything, and they don’t even have to touch your house.
Somebody took our water.
I’ll tell you about that later. It’s a long story and it has sugar in it.

We lived on a lane off Lahainaluna [lah-HY-nah-LOO-nah] Road, which runs straight up from the sea toward the old high school on the hill. Mauka [MOW-kah] of Front Street, we would say: toward the mountain. Here, nobody says north or south or east or west. You say mauka, toward the mountain, or makai [mah-KYE], toward the sea. Everything on this island is on its way from one to the other, and so are we.

The house was my grandfather’s. He cut cane for the sugar plantation for twenty years, and in 1940 he took the little money he’d saved and bought that house, a plantation house, wood on short posts, a green tin roof, three bedrooms, one bathroom, a lanai [lah-NYE] (that’s a porch) across the front where everybody’s slippers (that’s what we call flip-flops) piled up like a car crash. My mother was born in the back bedroom. I was born at the hospital in Wailuku [why-LOO-koo], the county town on the other side of the island, because my mother had some opinions about the back bedroom by then. My son, Keola [keh-OH-lah], was born in Wailuku too. He was eight that summer. Three of us in that house: my mother, me, my boy. Three generations, one bathroom. You learn to be quick.

My mother is Tūtū [TOO-too]. That means grandma, and everybody called her that, the whole lane, the guy at the gas station, the pastor, me. I called her Tūtū too, mostly, except when I was scared or arguing with her, which was most days. She was seventy-nine. She was small and brown and round, with white hair she wore pulled back with a pencil stuck through it, and she had a voice that could reach the end of the lane without trying. She had worked thirty years at the bank in town and then twenty more doing nothing she would admit was work: feeding people, raising my son, minding the whole street’s business from a plastic chair on the lanai.

In front of the house, by the gate, she grew a tree I have to tell you about, because it comes back. It was taller than the gate, thin-trunked, with big soft leaves, and it hung with flowers the size of my forearm. Long pale trumpets, cream and peach, that pointed straight down at the ground like they were ashamed of something. In the evening they gave off a smell, sweet and heavy, like somebody’s perfume left in a closed car. Tourists stopped to take pictures of it. Tūtū called it nānā honua [NAH-nah hoh-NOO-ah]. That means earth-gazing, because of how the flowers look down. In English they call it angel’s trumpet. It wasn’t from here. Somebody brought it, a long time ago, like they brought everything, and it liked our dirt and stayed.

“Every bit of that tree is poison,” Tūtū told Keola, the first day he could walk to the gate by himself. “The flowers, the leaves, the seeds. You eat it, you see things that aren’t there, and then you see nothing at all for good. You understand?”

He was three. He understood the way three-year-olds understand. He stood under it for an hour with his mouth shut tight, looking up at the hanging flowers like they were going to come down and get him.
“Then why do you keep it?” I asked her.
“Because it’s pretty,” she said. “And because somebody has to remember what pretty things can do.”
That was Tūtū. She talked like that, half proverb and half insult, and you never knew which half was meant for you.

I worked housekeeping at a resort in Kāʻanapali [kah-AH-nah-PAH-lee], about four miles up the coast. If you have been to Maui, you have probably stayed somewhere like it, and somebody like me cleaned your room, and you left her five dollars on the pillow, or you didn’t.

I’m not complaining. It was a good job. It had insurance. I had been there eleven years and I had a cart, my own cart, with my name taped on the handle, and I could turn over a king suite in twenty-two minutes on a good day, including the bathroom, including folding the end of the toilet paper into a little point so the guest feels like somebody cared.

Here is what I want you to see about Kāʻanapali. The resorts sit on a long gold beach with the island of Lānaʻi [lah-NAH-ee] floating across the water, and every morning before the guests wake up, the sprinklers come on. Hundreds of them. Thousands, maybe, if you count the golf course. They come up out of the grass with a little hiss and they turn and turn, throwing water in silver fans over lawns so green they look painted, and the light comes through the spray and makes small rainbows all over the property, and it is, honestly, one of the most beautiful things I have ever seen.
And then I would drive home, four miles, and look up.

Above the highway, all the way up the slope to where the rain begins, the land is brown. Not desert brown. Dead brown. The color of a paper bag. Grass up to your chest, dry as straw, crackling in the wind, mile after mile of it, right up to the edge of the town, right up to the back fences of the houses on the hill.
Green below. Brown above. The water knows which way it’s going. It always did. It’s just that somewhere along the way, somebody changed the address.
Let me tell you about my boy, and then I’ll stop for a while.

Keola means the life. He was born early, and small, and the doctor said he’d be fine, and he was more than fine, he was the loudest baby on the ward. His father left for Las Vegas when Keola was two, because a cousin had a job there and the rent here had gone where rents go when everybody wants to live on your island except the people who were born on it. So many of us have moved to Las Vegas they call it the ninth island. That’s a joke too. It isn’t funny either.

That summer Keola was eight and had lost both his front teeth at once, so he whistled when he talked. He was skinny and brown and fast, with hair that stood up in the back no matter what you put on it. And he could swim. Oh, he could swim. He swam before he could walk properly. Tūtū used to take him down to the harbor when he was two and hold him in the shallow water by the boat ramp, and he would kick and laugh and put his face right in it, and come up spitting and laughing more. By six he was jumping off the harbor wall with the big kids. By eight he was doing backflips off it, which I had told him not to do, which he did every afternoon, which I knew about, because the whole harbor knew about it and the whole harbor called me.

He was not afraid of the ocean. That’s what I’m saying. He was afraid of the angel’s trumpet tree, and of the dark hallway at night, and of Tūtū when she used his whole name. But the sea he trusted the way you trust your own bed.
I want you to remember that. I am telling you now, at the start, so that later you will know that I told you.
2. The Channel Wes
The first thing you notice, coming in, is that the water is the wrong color.

I say that as a man who has spent most of his life looking at water. I coach high-school swimming in a town in Ohio where the pool is the best-lit room in the county. I know chlorine blue, which is the blue of a painted box. I know Lake Erie in March, which is the color of a filing cabinet. I thought I knew what water was supposed to look like, and then the plane came down over the channel between Maui and the islands across from it, and I put my hand flat on the window like a kid.
It isn’t one color. That’s what I want to say, and I am going to take a minute to say it right, because I have never been good with words and I need to be good with these.

Near the shore, where the water is shallow over white sand, it is the palest green you have ever seen, so pale it is almost not a color, the green of the inside of a cucumber or of light through a glass bottle. A little farther out, where the sand drops and the reef begins, it turns turquoise, but a turquoise so bright it looks lit from underneath, as if somebody has hidden lamps on the bottom. Then there are patches, dark shapes like spilled ink, and those are the reefs themselves, coral and rock under ten or twenty feet of water, and over the patches the water goes the color of a bruise, purple and brown. And then, all at once, as if someone drew a line with a ruler, the bottom falls away into the deep, and the water goes a blue I have no name for. Not navy. Navy is a uniform. This was a blue that went down. A blue with weight in it. Looking at it from the plane I had the feeling you get at the edge of a high diving board, the feeling in the backs of your knees.

Across the channel the island of Lānaʻi sat low and long on the water like a sleeping animal, and behind it, farther off and fainter, the long dark ridge of Molokaʻi [moh-loh-KAH-ee], and all of it, every island, wore a cloud on its top like a hat.
“Theo,” I said. “Theo, look.”

My son was asleep against my arm with his mouth open. He was nine. He had his mother’s dark curls and her habit of sleeping with one hand in a fist under his chin like a boxer. I didn’t wake him. I looked at the water for both of us, and I tried to remember what Claire had said, fourteen years earlier, on this same approach, when we were twenty-nine and thirty and it was the first time either of us had been anywhere.
She had said, It looks like it’s breathing.
It did. It still did.
In the overhead bin above us, in my backpack, in a heavy plastic bag inside a cloth bag with a drawstring, were the ashes of my wife.

I’d like to say this the plain way, since there isn’t a fancy way. Claire got sick in the spring of the year Theo turned seven. Ovarian cancer, which is a cancer that hides until it is everywhere. She fought it for a year and a half with a kind of furious good manners. She died the September before this trip, at home, in the hospital bed we’d put where the dining table used to be, on a Tuesday afternoon with the window open because she wanted to hear the high school band practicing across the field.

She had asked for one thing. Lahaina was where we got married, barefoot on the beach, and where we spent our honeymoon, and she wanted to go into the sea there, from a boat, out in the channel where we had seen the whales. “Not in Ohio,” she said. “I’ve been cold in Ohio for forty-two years. Put me somewhere warm.”

So I had. I had brought her. I had argued with an airline about it on the phone for forty minutes. The crematorium had given me her ashes in a square box made of some dark wood, very handsome and very heavy, and I had left the box on the dresser at home, because I could not carry her through an airport in something that looked like a jewelry case. I took her out. I put her in the bag. I put the bag in my backpack between my running shoes and Theo’s inhaler. I am telling you this because I want you to know I am not a romantic man. I’m a practical man. I measure things. I think about weight.
My wife, all of her that was left, weighed a little over five pounds. I know because I put her on the kitchen scale. I’m not proud of it. I needed to know.

We were staying in a second-floor apartment on Front Street, which is the old main street of Lahaina, running along the water. I’d found it on one of the rental websites. The pictures showed a lanai with an ocean view, a kitchen with a pineapple-shaped cookie jar, two bedrooms, a ceiling fan with blades shaped like palm leaves. Walk to everything! Steps from the seawall! Sunsets you’ll never forget!

When I opened the door it smelled of somebody else’s cooking, years deep in the walls. There were pencil marks on the inside of the kitchen doorframe, painted over but still showing through the white, little lines with dates beside them, climbing up the wood. Somebody had measured their children here. Somebody had lived here for a long time before it became a place for people like me to sleep for a week.

I stood and looked at those marks longer than I should have. Theo dropped his bag on the floor and went straight to the lanai and stood at the railing, looking out across the street, across the low wall at the edge of the road, at the ocean.

It was right there. Thirty feet away. Front Street, then a seawall, black rocks piled against concrete, and then the water, slapping at the rocks, green-gold in the late sun, going out and out and out.
He stood there with both hands on the railing and didn’t move.
“Pretty great, huh, bud?”
“It’s really close,” he said.
“Yeah.”
“It’s really, really close.”
And I understood, the way you understand things about your child in your stomach before your head catches up, that he wasn’t admiring it. He was keeping an eye on it.
I should explain about Theo and the water, because it’s the thing I think about most, now, and because it was the great failure of my life before the other thing happened.

I am a swim coach. I’ve taught maybe a thousand children to swim. I can teach a scared six-year-old to put her face in the water in a single afternoon. I know the tricks. You blow bubbles. You count. You let them hold your hands and you never, ever let go until they tell you to. You make it a game. You make it boring, which is better than a game, because boring is the opposite of afraid.

Theo learned to swim when he was four, and he swam fine until he was seven. Then Claire got sick, and something happened inside him that I’ve never understood, and he stopped putting his face in. He’d go in the shallow end. He’d stand there. If the water came up past his chest his breathing changed, quick and high, a little catch at the top of every breath, and his eyes went somewhere far away. Deep water was worst. The bottom going away from under him. He said once, when I pushed him too hard at the Y, the YMCA pool back home, standing on the edge of the deep end in his trunks, shaking: “I can’t see what’s under it.”
I said, “There’s nothing under it, bud. It’s a pool. It’s twelve feet of nothing.”
He said, “That’s what I mean.”

I teach other people’s children. I couldn’t teach mine. I brought him to the most beautiful water on Earth, and part of the reason I did it, a part I didn’t say out loud even to myself, was that I thought maybe here, where his mother had been happy, the water would talk him round in a way I couldn’t.
I was a practical man. I’m telling you I had stopped being one.
3. Green Below, Brown Above Kanoe
Now I’ll tell you about the sugar, because you can’t understand what happened to us without it, and because nobody tells it on the T-shirts.

Go back two hundred years. Lahaina was the capital of the whole Hawaiian Kingdom then. Not Honolulu [hoh-noh-LOO-loo]. Here. Our kings and queens lived here, in the town of Lele, among the breadfruit trees, tall trees with big round fruit that tastes like bread when you cook it. There’s a phrase people still say, Ka malu ʻulu o Lele [kah MAH-loo OO-loo oh LEH-leh], the shade of the breadfruit trees of Lele. That’s what this town was. Shade. Cool green shade over the paths, and streams running through it, and taro fields stepped down toward the sea, flooded with water, shining like mirrors.

In the middle of the town there was a big pond, fed by springs and streams, called Mokuhinia [moh-koo-hee-NEE-ah]. And in the middle of the pond there was a small island called Mokuʻula [moh-koo-OO-lah]. It was the most sacred place in Lahaina. The king lived there, the third Kamehameha [kah-MAY-hah-MAY-hah], the one who ruled the longest, in the years when the whole world was arriving on his beach. His family was buried there. To reach him you crossed the water. Imagine that. A king on an island in a pond in a town full of streams, in the place we now call cruel sun.

Then the ships came. Whaling ships, from New England mostly, hundreds of them a year, anchored right out there in the channel where you see the snorkel boats now. That was the 1820s through the 1860s. The sailors came ashore for water and food and the things sailors come ashore for, and the town filled up with grog shops, which were the sailors’ bars, and fights and missionaries, all at the same time, and they did not like each other. That’s a whole other story. The missionaries built churches. The sailors once fired a cannon at a missionary’s house. Lahaina was the wild west, except it was the wild middle of the ocean.
The court moved to Honolulu in the 1840s. The whales got scarce, because the whalers had killed most of them. And then the sugar came.

Sugar cane is a tall grass. It is sweet, and it is thirsty, more thirsty than you can imagine. To grow a single pound of sugar you need around a ton of water. A ton. So the men who started the plantations here, and there were a few big companies that ended up owning most of West Maui, they did what you’d do if you needed a ton of water for every pound of sugar and you had money and the law was on your side. They went up the valleys and they dug ditches and tunnels into the mountain, and they caught the streams up high, and they turned them. They sent the water sideways along the slope, mile after mile, in ditches and flumes, which are wooden troughs on legs, to their fields.
The streams that used to run through Lahaina to the sea stopped running.

I don’t mean all at once. I don’t mean every drop. I mean that by the time my grandfather was a boy, the stream beds through town were dry most of the year, just rocks and weeds with a trickle in them after a big rain. The taro fields died. The springs that fed the royal pond got weak. The pond turned stagnant. Mosquitoes. Smell. And in the early part of the last century the county filled it in. They filled in the king’s pond with dirt and they put a baseball field on top of the sacred island.

It’s still there. A ballpark, with a dusty diamond and a chain-link backstop. Under the infield, under the pitcher’s mound, is Mokuʻula. You can go see. People are working to dig it back out. They have been working on it my whole life. It’s slow, digging up a king.

Everybody called the plantation the mill, after the building where the cane was crushed, and it ran in Lahaina for more than a hundred years. My grandfather worked there. Then my mother’s brothers. The mill whistle blew at shift change, and you could hear it all over town, and people set their clocks by it. Tūtū said when she was a girl the air at harvest smelled like burnt caramel, because before they cut the cane they burned the fields to clear the leaves, and the smoke came down over Lahaina sweet and black, and ash fell on the laundry. Black snow, they called it. Maui snow. The kids would run out and try to catch it on their tongues.

The mill closed in 1999. Sugar was cheaper to grow somewhere else, where the workers cost less. The fields went quiet. Nobody farmed them. And the plantation land, all those thousands of acres above the town, where the cane had been, filled up with grass.

Not our grass. Grass from Africa. Guinea grass, buffel grass, the kind of grass ranchers brought in a long time ago to feed cattle because it grows fast and doesn’t need much. It loves it here. It grows six feet tall in the wet months, and then it dries, and it stands there all summer like paper. Nobody grazes it. Nobody cuts it. It just stands there on the slope above Lahaina, mile after mile, right up to the fences, holding its breath.

When I was a kid, the mountain behind town was green with cane. When I was a woman it was gold with grass. When I was forty it was the color of a paper bag, and everybody on our lane knew what that color meant, and so did the fire department, and so did the people who make the laws, because it had already happened once.

August 2018. Five years before. There was a hurricane passing the island, Hurricane Lane, far out to sea, and it brought wind, big gusting wind that came down off the mountain, and a fire started up in the grass behind town, near Kauaʻula [kow-ah-OO-lah] Valley, and the wind pushed it down the hill into the houses.

It burned twenty-one homes. Twenty-one families. I knew three of them. We stood on the corner and watched the smoke go up from Kauaʻula, and Tūtū held Keola, who was three, and he said, “Is that a volcano?” and she said, “No, baby. That’s just grass.”

After that there were meetings. People came from the county and the state, and somebody had slides, and they talked about fire breaks, which are cleared strips a fire can’t cross, and fuel, and cutting back the grass, and the dry grass on the old plantation land, and everybody nodded. A few things got done. Not enough things. You know how it is. The grass grew back by the next summer, taller.
“Water,” Tūtū said, walking home from one of those meetings, leaning on my arm in the dark. “They don’t need a meeting. They need to give back the water.”
I said, “Mom, it’s not that simple.”
She stopped walking and looked at me. She did that, when she was about to be right.
“It was simple for a thousand years,” she said. “It got complicated when somebody started making money from it.”
4. The Boy Who Won’t Go Under Wes

On Friday I took Theo to the beach just south of town where the water is calm behind the reef. It’s a good beach for teaching. White sand, a gentle slope, water as clear as gin and warm as a bath. Little yellow fish, bright as lemon peel, nosing around your ankles. A sea turtle came in once while we were there, a big one, his shell the size of a car tire, and he cruised through the shallows ten feet from us and put his old wise face up out of the water and breathed out with a sound like a tired man sitting down, and went on.
Theo watched the turtle with his whole body. He loved it. He loved it from where he was, which was standing in water up to his knees.
“You want to swim out and see him?”
“No.”
“I’ll be right next to you.”
“No.”
“We could just put our faces in. Just for a second. With the goggles. You’d see all the fish.”
“I can see the fish from here.”

I know how to do this. I tell parents all the time: don’t push, don’t bribe, don’t make a fuss. Let the water be boring. So I let it be boring. I swam around in the shallows doing nothing. I lay on my back and floated, which is the thing I love most in the world, lying flat on the water with my ears under, hearing nothing but the click and hiss of the sea, looking up at a sky so big and blue it seemed to be coming down to meet me. Floating is the first thing I teach. Lie back, put your ears in, give the water your weight, it’ll give it back. It’s the first skill and it’s the last one. A person who can float is very hard to drown.

I looked over and Theo was sitting on the sand at the water’s edge with his knees pulled up, watching me float, with an expression I’d seen on his face only once before, in the doorway of the room where his mother was dying. It was the look of someone keeping watch.
I stood up and went in to him.
“Hey, bud.”
“Hey.”
“You want to go get shave ice?” Shave ice is ice shaved as fine as snow, with sweet syrup poured on top. Theo would walk a mile for it.
“Yeah.”
We didn’t talk about it. We never talked about it. That was a mistake. I made a lot of them. That one I’d take back first.
In the late afternoon we walked up Front Street to the banyan tree.

You need to see this tree, so I’ll try. It stands in a square in the middle of town by the old courthouse, and it isn’t a tree so much as a neighborhood. It was planted in 1873, I read on a plaque, a little sapling eight feet tall brought from India by the town sheriff to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the first missionaries arriving in Lahaina. A banyan grows strangely. It sends roots down out of its branches, thin as string at first, hanging in the air like hair, and when they touch the ground they take hold and thicken and become new trunks, so the tree walks outward, slowly, in every direction, holding itself up as it goes.

By the time we saw it, this one had something like sixteen trunks and covered most of the square. It was the biggest tree I’d ever been under. Its branches spread over the whole square on great gray arms held up by the trunks like a roof on pillars, and under it the light was green and dim and the air was ten degrees cooler, and there were benches and old men playing cards and kids running in and out between the trunks, and hundreds of birds, little brown mynahs, quarreling in the leaves with a sound like an argument in a crowded restaurant.
Theo walked in under it and looked up and said, “Whoa.” Which is what you say.

We sat on a bench. I bought him a mango smoothie. He drank it with both hands and I watched a man in his eighties at the next bench feed crumbs to a pigeon with enormous dignity, one crumb at a time, like he was dealing cards.
“Your mom and I sat here,” I said. “Right here. On our honeymoon.”
“On this bench?”
“Maybe. One of them. They all look the same.”
He looked at the bench as if it might have changed since then.
“Did she like it?”
“She loved it. She said it was like a church that grew itself.”
He thought about that for a while. Then he said, “Are we still doing the boat on Tuesday?”
“That’s the plan.”

The plan was this: on Tuesday morning a small charter boat would take us out into the channel, two miles off, where the water was deep, and I would open the bag and give Claire to the sea. I had paid for it in advance. It was the one thing on the calendar. The rest of the week was supposed to be just us, being here, the way she wanted.
“Will it be deep?” Theo said.
“Pretty deep.”
“How deep?”
I could have lied. I’ve thought about that a lot. “Couple hundred feet out there, maybe.”
He didn’t say anything. He put the straw back in his mouth and drank until it rattled at the bottom of the cup.

On the way back we cut down to the harbor. The small boat harbor in Lahaina is right in the middle of town, a square of calm water held in by a stone breakwater, full of fishing boats and charter boats and sailboats with their masts clicking in the wind like a hundred metronomes. At the end of the breakwater there’s a wall, maybe ten feet above the water, and that afternoon there was a gang of local kids on it, eight or ten of them, brown and skinny and shining wet, taking turns jumping off.

Not just jumping. Cannonballs. Spins. A big kid of maybe fourteen did a front flip with a scream that echoed off the boats. Then a little one stepped up. Couldn’t have been more than eight, all knees and elbows, his hair standing straight up at the back like a duck’s tail. He looked over his shoulder at the bigger kids to make sure they were watching. They were. He bent his knees, swung his arms, and threw himself backward off the wall, head over heels, a full backflip, and went into the water feet first with hardly a splash.
The big kids went wild. Theo, next to me, grabbed my arm so hard it hurt.

The little one came up laughing, spat out a mouthful of the harbor, and swam back to the ladder like a seal, quick and easy, his face in the water every stroke, not bothering to look where he was going because he didn’t need to. He climbed up, dripping, and walked right past us on his way back to the wall. He was missing both his front teeth. He saw Theo staring and grinned at him, a big gappy grin.
“Your boy no like swim, Uncle?” he said to me. It came out with a whistle through the gap.
I didn’t understand right away. “Sorry?”
“He scared?” The kid pointed at Theo, not unkindly. “Water’s nice. Come.” He pointed down at the harbor. “Warm. Like one bath.”
Theo shook his head, a small, fast shake.
The kid shrugged, the way kids do, your loss, and ran back to the wall and jumped again.
“Why did he call you Uncle?” Theo asked me, on the walk home.

I didn’t know. I found out later that it’s what kids here call any grown man, any grown man at all, a stranger, the mailman, a tourist from Ohio. Uncle. Auntie. Everybody is somebody’s family. It’s a courtesy. It’s also a statement about how the world is supposed to work.
I didn’t know that then. I just said, “I guess it’s a nice thing.”
“I liked him,” Theo said.
“Yeah?”
“He wasn’t scared of anything.”
5. Red Flag Kanoe
That week the wind started talking about something.

You learn the wind here the way you learn a person’s moods. Most days the trade winds come from the northeast, steady and cool, pushing the clouds onto the mountain where they drop their rain, and then slide down our side warm and dry. That’s normal. That’s the island breathing. But that week, at the start of August, there was a hurricane far to the south, a big one, called Dora. It never came near us. It passed hundreds of miles away, way down under the island, going west. And at the same time there was a big area of high pressure sitting far up to the north.

I’m not a scientist. Here’s how my mother explained it, and it’s good enough. “When you have a big push up there and a big pull down there,” she said, holding up one fist high and one fist low, “the wind runs between them like water downhill. And we’re in the way.”

On Monday, the seventh, the weather people put out a warning. A red flag warning, they call it. That’s the warning they give when it’s dry and windy and any spark will run. They said the winds would be bad Monday night and Tuesday. Gusts of sixty miles an hour, they said. Maybe more on the slopes. They said to secure loose objects. They said the humidity was low, which means the air was dry as paper. They said, in the gentle way they say it, any fires that develop will likely spread rapidly.

I read it at work on my phone during my lunch break, sitting on an upside-down bucket behind the laundry. Then I put my phone in my pocket and went back to work. That’s what you do. I had nine more rooms.

By afternoon you could feel it. The palms in the resort were bending over, all their fronds streaming one way like hair in front of a fan, and the sound they made was a long dry rush, like a crowd going shhhh. The pool attendants were running around collecting towels before they blew into the ocean. A beach umbrella came loose and went cartwheeling down the lawn like a drunk on a bicycle, and three of the boys from the activities desk chased it, laughing.

The sea was white. Usually from the resort the channel is blue and flat, Lānaʻi sitting on it like a plate on a table. That afternoon the whole channel was scratched with whitecaps, thousands of them, as far as you could see, and the wind tore the tops off the waves and blew them sideways in little ghosts of spray.
The sprinklers came on at five. I watched the water fly out of them and the wind catch it and carry it, every drop, sideways off the lawn and away into nothing before it touched the grass.

I got home at six. Tūtū was on the lanai in her plastic chair with a wet towel round her neck. Keola was in the yard with a soccer ball, kicking it against the wall of the house over and over, bam, bam, bam, which was his way of saying he was bored and the wind was making him crazy, which it makes everybody.
“Stop that,” Tūtū said, without looking at him. He stopped. He started again a minute later. She didn’t say anything that time.

The angel’s trumpet was thrashing by the gate. The wind had torn off a lot of the flowers and they were lying in the dirt and on the walk, pale and bruised. The smell was everywhere, stronger than I’d ever smelled it, that thick sweet perfume, all of it shaken loose at once and blowing up onto the lanai.
“Smells like a funeral,” I said.
“Smells like a party,” Tūtū said. “Depends who’s invited.”
I sat down on the step below her and she put her hand on my head, the way she used to when I was little. Her hand was cool from the wet towel.
“The wind,” she said, “is going to bring the power lines down tonight.”
“Probably.”
“You charge your phone?”
“Yes, Mom.”
“Charge it again.”
Here is a thing about my mother that I didn’t know I would need to tell anybody, until I needed to.

That night she told Keola a story at bedtime. She did it most nights. He was eight and pretended to be too old for it, and he still lay there in the dark with his eyes open waiting for her to start. I was in the kitchen doing dishes by the light of the stove clock, and through the open door I could hear her voice going low and steady, the voice she saved for him.

She told him about the water. She did that a lot. She told him about the streams that used to run through town to the sea, and the taro fields, and the king on his island in the pond. She told him how the king, when he was small, younger than Keola, used to swim across to his island instead of taking the canoe, because he liked to arrive wet. She told him how the streams, before they were turned, would come down from the mountain after a rain so loud you could hear them in your sleep, and in the morning the whole town would wake up to the sound of water running, everywhere, like the town itself was laughing.
“Where did the water go, Tūtū?” he asked her. He had heard the story a hundred times. He always asked.

“Same place it always goes,” she said. “Down. To the sea. The water always goes home. They can turn it, they can put it in a pipe, they can sell it, but in the end, every drop, every single drop, it comes home to the ocean. And the ocean remembers every drop that ever came. Every one. That’s why it’s salty. It’s all the tears and all the rivers and all the rain that ever was, and it keeps them all. It doesn’t forget anything.”
“Does it remember me?”
“You,” she said, “it knows by name.”

I stood at the sink with my hands in the dishwater, not washing anything. Outside, the wind was getting louder. The tin roof was rattling at one corner where a nail had worked loose years ago and nobody had fixed it.
“Night, Tūtū.”
“Good night, my life.”
She called him that. My life. It’s what his name means. She was the only one who said it in English.
6. The Night the Wind Came Wes
The power went out at about ten.

I was lying in bed in the dark in the back bedroom, listening. The wind had been building all evening, and by ten it wasn’t wind anymore, it was weather. It came off the mountain behind town in long screaming gusts that shook the whole building, and between the gusts there were pauses, a second or two of strange quiet, and then the next one would hit, harder, and something outside would bang and clatter down the street. Somebody’s trash can. Somebody’s patio chair. A palm frond the size of a canoe paddle hit our sliding door with a crack like a gunshot and I sat straight up in bed with my heart going.

Then the ceiling fan, which had been turning slowly over my head, slowed. Wound down. Stopped. The little green light on the smoke detector went out. The refrigerator in the kitchen gave a last shudder and fell silent, and in that silence I realized how much I’d been hearing it.

I got up and went out to the living room and looked through the sliding door. Front Street was black. The whole town was black. No street lamps, no windows, no neon from the bars up the street. Just the wind and, above it, a sky so full of stars it looked spilled. I’d never seen so many. Ohio has a stingy sky. This one had been opened like a sack of sugar and poured out from edge to edge, the
Milky Way a pale smoke right across the middle, and the stars weren’t still, they were trembling, every one of them, the way stars do when the air is moving fast.

Under the stars the sea was making a sound I hadn’t heard it make before. Not the soft slap and suck of the afternoon. A deep, steady roar, the waves coming in hard against the seawall across the street, boom and then a long rattling hiss as the water fell back through the rocks, boom, hiss, boom. It sounded like something very big breathing in its sleep.

I stood at the glass and looked at the dark water I couldn’t see, only hear, and I thought: Claire would have loved this. She liked storms. She’d stand on the back porch in Ohio in thunderstorms with a beer, getting rained on, while I stood in the doorway asking her to please come in before she got struck by lightning.
The bag of her was on the dresser in the bedroom. I’d taken it out of the backpack that night. I don’t know why. I think I wanted her in the room.
After a while I went back to bed. At some point, I heard Theo’s door open.
He came down the little hall in the dark in his pajamas and stood in my doorway. I couldn’t see his face. Just his shape, small and thin, and the white of his T-shirt.
“Dad.”
“Hey, bud. Just the wind. Power’s out. It’s okay.”
“It’s loud.”
“I know. Want to come in?”

He came in. He climbed up into the big bed on Claire’s side, which was what we called the left side of any bed, still, even hotel beds. He hadn’t slept in my bed since the first month after she died. He lay down with his back against me, and I put my arm over him, and I could feel his heart going like a bird’s.
The building shook. Something heavy rolled down Front Street outside, clanging.
“Dad?”
“Yeah.”
“Is the ocean going to come in?”
“No, bud. It’s just wind. The ocean’s staying where it is.”
“How do you know?”
I didn’t know. I said, “Because the wall’s there. That’s what the wall’s for. To keep the ocean on its side.”
He was quiet for a while. I thought he’d fallen asleep. Then he said, so quietly I almost didn’t hear him over the wind:
“Is Mom going in tomorrow?”
I had forgotten. That’s the truth. With the wind and the dark I had completely forgotten that tomorrow, Tuesday, was the boat.
“If the boat can go out,” I said. “If the wind’s this bad, maybe not. We’ll see in the morning.”
“Okay.” A pause. “Dad?”
“Yeah.”
“Will she be scared? In the deep part?”

I lay there with my arm around my son, in the dark, in a stranger’s apartment with the marks of a stranger’s children on the doorframe, with my wife in a bag on the dresser, and I didn’t have an answer. I’m a coach. I’m supposed to always have an answer. Bend your knees. Tuck your chin. Breathe on every third stroke.
“No,” I said. “She won’t be scared. She’ll be warm. That’s what she wanted. She was always cold.”
“Okay.”
“Go to sleep, bud.”

He did, eventually. I didn’t. I lay awake listening to the wind try to take the roof off, and to the sea breathing against the wall, and every time a gust came I tightened my arm round him a little without meaning to, the way you grip the edge of something when you lose your footing.

Around four I must have dozed, because I dreamed. I won’t tell you most of it. I’ll tell you only that in the dream I was floating on my back in very warm, very dark water, with my ears under, and I could hear, through the water, somebody talking. A woman’s voice. Low and steady. Telling a story to someone. I couldn’t make out the words. I just knew from the sound of it that it was a story you tell a child at night, to keep them from being afraid of the dark.
Said at the Reef

You are afraid of me. That’s all right. Most of your kind are, at first. You come from the land, and the land is a floor, and I am not a floor. I am the opposite of a floor. I am the place where the floor goes away.
But listen. Lie still a moment and let me tell you where you are, because a thing is less frightening once you know its name.

You are on the west side of an island that a fire built. Long ago, so long that the number would mean nothing to you, the earth under this ocean opened a wound that never closed, and melted rock came up through it, and through me, hissing, boiling me as it rose, and it cooled into mountains. I was there. I held it while it hardened. I have held every island in this chain from the day it came up out of the dark, and I will hold each one when it goes back down, because they all go back down. That is a secret about islands. They are only visiting.

The rain made the island green. That is my doing too. I rise off the sea as warm breath, invisible, and the trade wind carries me to the mountain, and the mountain pushes me up into the cold, and I turn back into myself and fall. On top of the mountain behind this town it rains more than in almost any place in the world. Up there I live in the moss. I live in the ferns, in the long silver threads of waterfalls that hang off the cliffs like rope. Then I gather myself in the valleys and I run down. That is all I have ever wanted to do. Run down. Come home.

Before your kind of people came, the people who were here understood that. They made their lives in the shape of my running. They cut their land in slices that followed my streams, from the cloud to the reef, so that every family could stand somewhere along my path and dip their hands in me. They grew their taro in pools of me, terrace after terrace stepping down the slope, each one spilling into the next, the way you might pass a full cup down a table. They let me reach the sea. That was the rule, and it was the only rule that mattered: whatever you take, let some of it get home.
Look down. You can see it from here. The reef.

It is alive, all of it. What looks like stone is a city of tiny animals, each one smaller than a grain of rice, each one building itself a little cup of white stone out of me, out of what I carry, and living in the cup, and dying in it, and leaving it for the next one to build on. A thousand years of that and you have a reef. Ten thousand and you have this. Green and gold and violet, built like a cathedral by creatures that never knew they were building anything. Fish move through it in clouds. Yellow ones, bright as a lemon cut open. Blue ones that turn silver when they turn. A long thin one, like a needle, that hangs at the surface and watches. In the winter the whales come down from the cold north and sing in this channel, and the songs carry through me for miles, and the people on the shore put their heads under me to hear, and for a little while they are quiet.

Some of you give me your weight the way a man hands over a sleeping child. Not many. Most of you hold yourselves up. You stiffen. You keep your face out of me and your eyes on the bottom, and when the bottom goes away you feel it in your knees and your stomach, and you go back to where you can stand. I don’t blame you. Most of you have lost a floor once already, somewhere in your life, and have been standing very carefully ever since, testing every step.
I understand that. I lost my floor too, in a way. I’ll tell you about it. Not yet. There’s time. Tonight there’s nothing but time.

For now I want you only to know this one thing. Everything that has ever come down to me, I’ve kept. Every drop of rain. Every river. Every tear anybody ever cried on this beach. They are all still here, in me, not lost, only mixed. Somewhere in this channel, right now, is the water that once ran through the king’s pond. Somewhere is the sweat of the men who cut the cane. Somewhere is the rain that fell on this island the day it rose. I don’t forget. I can’t. It isn’t in me to forget.
That’s what the old woman on the hill told her grandson every night. She was right. She usually was.
Lie still. You’re all right. I’ve got you.
II. DECLARED CONTAINED
7. Contained Kanoe
The alarm on my phone went at five-fifteen and the phone was the only light in the house.

The power was still out. It had gone out around ten the night before and it had not come back. The wind hadn’t stopped all night. It had found every gap in the old house, every loose board, every crack around the window frames, and it had whistled through them in different notes like a broken church organ. The loose corner of the tin roof had banged until two in the morning and then, suddenly, stopped, which meant either the nail had gone back in by itself or the piece of roof had gone to Lānaʻi.

I dressed in the dark. In the kitchen I could hear Tūtū breathing from the back bedroom, a little whistle at the end of every breath, the way she did when she was in deep. I didn’t wake her. I left a note on the counter under the rice cooker, which was where we left notes. No power. Went work. Charge phone in car if you need. Love you. I looked in on Keola. He was asleep sideways across his bed with one foot hanging off the edge and his mouth open, and the wind was pushing the curtain in over him, out, in, out, like the room was breathing.

I almost didn’t go to work. I want to say that, because later I counted every almost. I stood in the doorway of his room and thought: it’s a bad day, the power’s out, no school, just stay home. Then I thought about my nine rooms, and about my supervisor, who was a nice man who was not nice about attendance. And the resort would have generators. Somebody had to be there for the guests, who would be hot and angry and wanting coffee.

So I went. I kissed the top of my boy’s head and he didn’t wake up, and I went out past the angel’s trumpet, whose flowers were all over the ground now, smashed and brown and still smelling, and I got in the car and drove up the coast in the dark, under trees that were bending nearly to the road.

The last thing I saw of my house, the way it was, was in the rear-view mirror: just a dark shape, and the tree thrashing by the gate, and the long brown slope of the mountain behind it, black against a sky that was starting to go gray.

The resort was in chaos, the polite kind. The generators were running the kitchens and the front desk and some of the hallway lights, but not the air conditioning in the rooms, and not the elevators in the tower. Guests were coming down the stairs in their bathrobes looking for coffee and an explanation. I gave them neither. I was a housekeeper. I smiled and said, “So sorry, ma’am, I don’t know. Front desk might know,” and I went up the stairs with my cart, which I had to leave at the bottom, carrying my towels and sheets up six flights in a laundry bag on my back like Santa Claus.
At ten to seven my phone buzzed in my pocket. A text from my cousin, who lived two streets over from us.
fire up lahainaluna by the school. firemen there. u ok?
I stopped on the stairs between the fourth and fifth floors with the bag on my back and called home. It rang and rang. I called again. Tūtū answered on the fifth ring, sounding cross.
“What?”
“Mom. There’s a fire up the road.”
“I know. I can see it. I’m standing in the yard.”
“Is it close?”

“It’s up by the school. The grass is burning. Fire trucks are there, three, four. Lot of smoke. Lot of wind.” I could hear the wind in the phone, a roar like the phone was pressed against a seashell. “Police came down the lane, said maybe go, just in case.”
“Then go! Take Keola and go!”
“I’m going, I’m going. Don’t shout at me. Auntie Rose is picking us up. We’ll go to her place by the harbor till it’s done.”
Auntie Rose was not my aunt. Auntie Rose was the woman who’d lived across the lane for forty years and then moved down near the harbor when her husband died. Everybody’s family, I told you.
“Call me when you’re there.”

“I’ll call you, I’ll call you. Go do your work. Bye. Love you.” And she hung up, because Tūtū never in her life stayed on a phone call one second longer than she had to. She thought phones were rude. She said if you wanted to tell somebody you loved them, you should go stand in front of them.

She called back at eight-twenty. They were at Auntie Rose’s. Keola was eating cereal with no milk, because there was no cold milk, there was no cold anything in the whole town. The smoke was going the other way, out over the hills, she said, the wind pushing it. And then a little before ten my cousin texted again.
they saying contained

And a little after that I saw it on my phone too, the county had put it out, the fire in Lahaina was contained. Contained means the firefighters have got a line around it, a ring of dug-out dirt and wet ground, so it can’t get out and spread. Later they would say it was out. Fully out. I read the word, contained, standing in a guest’s bathroom with a toilet brush in my hand, and I felt my whole body come down off its toes.
Tūtū called at eleven. She sounded tired.
“They’re letting people back. Keola wants his ball. We’re walking home.”
“Mom, is that smart? Just stay at Rose’s.”

“Rose has one ceiling fan and it doesn’t work, and she talks. I’m going home. The fire’s out. The firemen are up there, they’re watching it. I talked to one of them, nice boy, he’s Leilani’s [lay-LAH-nee] nephew. He said the fire’s dead.”
“Okay.”

“You know what he said? He said they were lucky. He said if the wind had turned they’d have been in trouble, because half the trucks on the island are upcountry, up on the big mountain, at the other fire.” She laughed a little. “Not enough fire trucks. Plenty of sprinklers in Kāʻanapali, though.”
“Mom.”
“I’m just saying what the boy said.” A pause. Wind. “Your son is pulling my arm. He wants to talk to you.”
Keola came on. He was out of breath. “Mom! There was a fire! By the school! I saw the fire truck! It was so big!”
“I know, baby. I’m glad you’re safe.”
“The wind blew Auntie Rose’s chair into the harbor! The whole chair!”
“Wow.”
“Can I go swim later?”
“No. Not today. It’s too windy. The water’s rough. Stay with Tūtū.”
“Aw.”
“Keola.”
“Okay,” he said. “Bye. Love you.” Exactly like his grandmother, three words and gone.
I stood in that guest’s bathroom for a minute after he hung up, looking at the phone. Then I went back to work. I did all nine rooms. I folded the end of every toilet paper roll into a point.

I tell you this so you know how ordinary it was. A fire up the road, and then it was out. That’s how the morning went. That’s how it ends, usually. Out here, a grass fire in a high wind is nothing new. It burns, the trucks come, it gets put out, and you go home and you sweep the ash off the lanai and you say that was close and you have a beer.
That’s what we thought. That’s what everybody thought. The trucks thought it. The county thought it. The wind did not think it, but nobody asked the wind.
8. No Boat Today Wes
The charter company texted at seven: Due to high winds all tours cancelled today. Full refund or reschedule. Mahalo for understanding!

I read it twice. I didn’t know what mahalo [mah-HAH-loh] meant. I found out later it means thank you. I didn’t feel thankful. I felt, I’m ashamed to say, relieved, and then I felt bad about the relief, because it meant another day of carrying her. I looked at the bag on the dresser and thought: one more day, Claire. Sorry. The wind.

The power was still out. No coffee. The refrigerator, when I opened it, breathed out warm. The milk I’d bought on Sunday smelled fine but felt wrong, like milk that had been somewhere without me. I gave Theo a granola bar and a banana and a juice box, and we ate them on the lanai, sitting on the floor with our backs to the wall because the wind was too strong to stand up in comfortably. It came off the mountain behind us, over the roof of our building, and went straight out to sea, and it was hot, which surprised me. You think of wind as cooling. This wind was warm and dry, like the air from a hair dryer, and it took the moisture out of your eyes and the inside of your nose until everything stung.

Out over the channel the sea was white to the horizon. The wind was tearing the tops off the waves and carrying the spray away in long smoking streaks, so it looked as if the whole surface of the ocean were on fire with white flames, all streaming in one direction, away from the island. Lānaʻi was gone behind a haze. The sky above it was blue and perfectly clear and somehow wrong.
“It’s really windy,” Theo said.
“Sure is.”
“Is the boat going?”
“Not today. Tomorrow maybe.”
He nodded. I watched him. He looked out at the white water for a while and then he said, very carefully, “Okay,” and I knew that he was relieved too. Neither of us said it.
Around eight we saw the smoke.

It was behind us, up the hill, over the rooftops on the other side of Front Street. A brown column going up and then, very quickly, bending flat, the wind catching it and stretching it out over the town toward the sea, so it passed right over us, high up, a long brown smear across the blue. I could smell it. Grass smoke. Like a field burning in October back home.

People came out onto the street. A woman from the apartment downstairs, in a T-shirt that said Lahaina Is My Happy Place, stood on the sidewalk with her hand over her eyes. A man in a fishing hat said it was up by the high school. He said there were trucks there. He said, “Happens all the time, brah, with this wind,” and I didn’t know if brah [BRAH], which I learned later just means brother, was for me or for the woman, but it was friendly and it calmed me down.

By ten it was gone. The smoke thinned and stopped. The man in the fishing hat came back down the street and said, “They got it,” and gave a thumbs-up, and the woman in the Happy Place shirt clapped, and everybody went back inside to not have air conditioning.

That was the morning fire. I’ve read everything about it since. I have read reports and timelines and the testimony of people who were there, and I’ve read it the way a man reads the last page of a book first, knowing how it ends, looking for the moment it could have gone the other way. I’ll tell you plainly what I learned, since nobody told me then.

The fire started at about six-thirty-five in the morning, in tall dry grass at the side of Lahainaluna Road, the road that goes straight up the hill from town to the old school. Earlier, the wind had snapped the power lines there, and then the power came back on into the broken wires. A power line carries enough electricity to light a town. When a live broken end touches the grass, even for a second, it throws sparks and melted metal like a welder’s torch. The grass caught. The wind pushed it. The firefighters came quickly and fought it, and they held it, and around the middle of the morning they announced it was contained, and then that it was out.

But a fire in grass isn’t like a fire in a fireplace. It’s not just flames you can see. It gets down into the roots and the dead stalks matted near the ground, into the dirt itself, and it can sit there smoldering, hidden, hot, without any flame at all, for hours. Firefighters have a name for this. They call it a holdover. And they have a job for it too: after the flames are gone, they walk the burned ground with hand tools, turning the dirt, feeling with the backs of their bare hands for heat, soaking every hot spot until the ground is cold. It’s called mop-up. It’s slow and filthy and boring, and it is the most important part of the job.

That morning, the Maui Fire Department was stretched across the whole island. In the middle of the night another fire had started upcountry, in a place called Kula [KOO-lah], on the slopes of the big mountain on the other side of Maui, and it was burning toward houses there, and engines had gone. Firefighters were moving between fires. The wind was knocking down poles and lines all over the island, and every downed line was a new chance of fire.

A little after two in the afternoon, the crew watching the Lahaina burn left the scene. It was the right call by everything they could see. The fire was out. That was the information. The information was wrong.

We went out at noon, because the apartment was an oven. Front Street was strange. Most of the shops were closed with handwritten signs on the doors, NO POWER, SORRY, CLOSED, and a few were open with their doors propped wide, dim inside, selling whatever didn’t need electricity. A woman at a fruit stand sold us two mangoes and a bag of something she called li hing [LEE hing] dried plums, which were sweet and sour and salty all at once and made Theo pull a face and then ask for more. She took cash only, no card machines. Everybody was talking about the wind. Everybody had a story: a tree down on their road, a roof gone, a boat dragging its anchor in the harbor.
We walked up to the banyan. I wanted to show Theo the tree in the wind. I’m not sure why. Maybe because Claire would have.

It was something. The great tree was alive with it. The thousands of branches were heaving, the leaves showing their pale undersides all at once in waves, silver-green, silver-green, so the whole crown of the tree seemed to ripple like water. And the sound. Under the banyan, in that wind, it sounded like being inside the ocean, a vast steady roar of leaves with the cracking of small branches in it, and the mynah birds screaming. The hanging roots were swinging like ropes in a gym. Twigs and leaves were raining down. The old men with the cards were gone. Nobody was under there but us and a few tourists taking videos on their phones.
Theo stood in the middle of it with his arms out and his eyes shut, letting the wind push him. He was smiling. It was the first time I’d seen him smile with his whole face since we landed.
“It feels like flying!” he shouted.
“Yeah!”
“Do you think Mom sat here?”
“Right about here!”
He opened his eyes and looked at me. “Can we do the boat tomorrow?”
“If the wind stops.”
“Okay.” He shut his eyes again and leaned into the wind. “I think I want to go,” he shouted. “On the boat. I want to see the deep part. For Mom.”

I didn’t say anything. I couldn’t. I just stood next to him in the roaring green dark under that tree and nodded, which he couldn’t see because his eyes were shut, and I put my hand on the back of his neck, which was hot and damp, and I left it there.
That was about two o’clock.
9. Go Work Kanoe

At two I took my break on the bucket behind the laundry with a can of warm guava juice and checked my phone. One bar. No messages. I called home. It rang, and rang, and then a woman’s recorded voice said the call couldn’t be completed. I tried again. Same thing.
I wasn’t worried yet. The cell towers had been going in and out all day. Half my texts were coming through an hour late, out of order, like mail delivered by a drunk.
I texted: Mom you ok?
The little circle turned and turned. Then: Not delivered.
I’m going to tell you something I saw that afternoon, which I didn’t think about at the time but which I’ve thought about every day since.

From the laundry dock at the back of the resort you can see down the coast, south, toward Lahaina. Four miles. On a clear day you can see the harbor and the white steeple of the church and the dark green bump that is the banyan tree. That afternoon the wind had blown the air so clean that I could see all of it, sharp, like a photograph. And above the town, up the slope, there was the brown burned patch from the morning fire, a dark scar on the gold grass by Lahainaluna Road.
I looked at it. I remember thinking that it was smaller than I thought it would be. I remember being glad.
And I remember that there was a little gray haze hanging over it. Not smoke. Not really. More like the air over a road on a hot day, wavering.
I looked at that and I went back inside and did my last two rooms.

I have tried, since, to remember if I knew. If some part of me looked at that wavering air and knew what it was. I don’t think so. I think I just saw a hot day. That’s what everybody saw. The haze above a burned field in the wind, a little shimmer. That’s all a holdover looks like, from four miles away. It looks like nothing.
At twenty past three, my supervisor came down to the laundry. His name doesn’t matter. He was a nice man. His face was a color I’d never seen it.
“Kanoe,” he said. “You’re from Lahaina, yeah? Lahainaluna side?”
“Yeah.”
“You should go look.”
He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t have to. I walked out past him onto the loading dock and I looked down the coast, and the photograph had changed.

There was smoke over Lahaina. Not a column, like the morning. A wall. It was coming up from the town, from the slope above the town, from right where the morning’s burned patch had been, black and brown and moving fast, and the wind was taking it, bending the top of it out over the sea in a long dark arm that stretched across the channel toward Lānaʻi, getting wider and wider until it was a curtain, a black curtain pulled across the bottom of the sky. Under it, at the bottom, at the root of the smoke, I could see the color. You know the color. I don’t have to tell you.
I took out my phone. One bar. I called home.
It rang.
It rang.
A recorded voice.
I called Auntie Rose. Recorded voice.
I called my cousin. It rang once and went dead.
I texted: MOM FIRE GET OUT GO TO THE HARBOR GO NOW
The little circle turned and turned.
Not delivered.

I don’t remember deciding to go. I remember my keys in my hand, and the parking structure, and my car, and pulling out onto the highway headed south, and the sky in front of me so dark that every car on the road had its headlights on, at half past three in the afternoon, little yellow lights pushing into the dark.

The wind was hitting the car from the side so hard I had to hold the wheel with both hands. Dust and leaves and pieces of things were flying across the road. A sheet of roofing tin went over the car, flipping, flashing, like a giant playing card. Ahead of me, cars were stopped. Not slowing. Stopped. Brake lights all the way down the highway into the smoke, and people standing outside their cars, and a police car with its lights going sideways across both lanes.
The road into Lahaina was closed.

I got out and ran up to the policeman. He was young. He had a mask over his mouth and his eyes were red and streaming. I don’t remember what I said. I remember he put his hand up flat, palm out, the way you’d stop a dog.
“Ma’am, nobody’s going in. Road’s closed. It’s not safe.”
“My son is in there. My mother. Lahainaluna. Off Lahainaluna.”
“Ma’am.”
“My son is eight.”
He looked at me then. Just for a second, over the mask. He was crying, I realized. It wasn’t the smoke. Or it was the smoke and also it wasn’t.
“Ma’am,” he said, “I’ve got a kid too. I’m sorry. I’m sorry. Nobody’s going in.”

I stood at that roadblock for an hour. I don’t know what I did for an hour. I know that sometime around four the wind came down the highway carrying a sound I’d never heard before and never want to again: from inside the smoke, from somewhere in the town, a long rolling series of bangs, pop, pop, pop-pop-pop, like fireworks on New Year’s, like a war in a movie.
That was cars. I found out later. That was the gas tanks of cars blowing up, one after another, all down Front Street.
10. The Hill Is Smoking Wes
Just after three, walking back down Front Street toward the apartment, Theo stopped and pointed up over the rooftops behind the town.
“Dad. The fire’s back.”

I looked. Over the buildings, up the hill, where the morning smoke had been, there was smoke again. Gray at first, and thin, just a few wisps leaning out flat in the wind like a flag. Then, while I watched, it thickened. It turned brown. It turned black at the bottom. It came up in a fat rolling column that the wind caught at once and laid down sideways over the top of the town, right over our heads, so the sun went orange and then went out, and the light on Front Street changed in a single second from white to the color of weak tea.
Somebody on the sidewalk said, “Oh, no.”

There’s a moment, when something terrible begins, when your body knows and your mind doesn’t, and you stand there in between, like a man who’s stepped off a curb he didn’t know was there. I stood there. I held Theo’s hand and looked up at the smoke going over and I thought: it’s the morning fire again. They’ll get it. That’s what they do. The man in the fishing hat will come down the street and give a thumbs-up.

And something else in me, something below the thinking part, something that had stood on the edges of pools for twenty years watching for the one kid in a hundred who was in trouble before that kid knew it, said: Get out of the water. Get out of the water right now.
I’m going to slow down here. I’m going to tell you the next part carefully, the way I’ve told it to myself every night since, because if I go fast I’ll lose it.

We went back to the apartment. That’s what you do. You go home. I don’t know why. You go home to get your things, your wallet, your phone charger, your ID, your kid’s inhaler, your wife. I unlocked the door with my hands shaking. Inside it was dim and hot. Through the sliding door the sea was a strange dark green under the smoke, and the white streaks on it had turned orange, every one of them, reflecting the sky.
I put Theo on the couch. “Stay right there. Shoes on. Don’t move.”

I went to the bedroom and grabbed the backpack. I put in my wallet. Phone. The inhaler. The rental car keys, though the car was parked in a lot six blocks north and I didn’t know if I’d be able to get to it. Two bottles of water. And then I stood at the dresser, with the bag of my wife sitting there in front of me, and I picked her up, all five pounds of her, and I put her in the backpack on top of everything else, and I zipped it, and I put it on.

I’m a practical man. I knew exactly what I was doing. I knew that if I had to choose between carrying my son and carrying my wife, I would put her down. I knew that. I took her anyway, because I wasn’t going to leave her in a stranger’s apartment in a burning town. I’d promised her somewhere warm. Not like this. Not this kind of warm.
When I came out Theo was standing at the sliding door with his hands flat on the glass, looking out at the water.
“Theo. Come on. We’re going.”
“Where?”
“To the car.”
“Is the fire coming here?”
“I don’t know, bud. We’re going anyway. Come on.”

He came. I took his hand. It was wet and cold, even in that heat. We went down the stairs and out onto Front Street, and the street had changed again while we were inside, like a stage when the lights change between scenes.

It was dark now. Not night dark. A brown dark, smoke dark, with a red light under it coming from somewhere up the hill behind the buildings, so that everything, the cars, the sidewalk, the people, the palm trees, had a red edge on one side, the way things look by firelight in a cave. The air tasted of burning, bitter on the back of the tongue. Ash was falling. Not big pieces yet. A fine gray snow, drifting sideways, settling on Theo’s curls and on my arms.

And there were people everywhere. Everybody had come out at once. People in cars, in a long line already, honking, not moving. People on foot with bags, with dogs, with babies, with a birdcage, with a TV. An old man pushing a woman in a wheelchair down the middle of the street, the wheelchair’s little front wheels catching on every crack. Kids crying. A woman screaming a name over and over, Mika! Mika! [MEE-kah], into the smoke.

And the sound. Under all the voices, under the honking, the wind. And under the wind, from up the hill, something else, a deep rumbling roar, like a freight train that never arrived, that just kept coming.

What I didn’t hear was a siren. Not a warning siren. I heard car alarms, and somewhere a police car, and dogs, and people. But I’d seen the warning sirens on the poles around town, big gray horns on top of tall posts, the kind they have all over Hawaii for tsunamis, for anything. I’d noticed them on the first day and thought, that’s good, they’ve got a system. They did. There were a lot of them, all along the west side.
Not one of them went off. Not that day.

I didn’t think about it then. I didn’t think about anything. I just held my son’s hand and turned north up Front Street toward the parking lot where the car was, into the brown dark, through the falling ash, with my wife on my back.
Said in the Stream Bed
Let me tell you how I lost my floor. I said I would.

Up behind this town, in the folds of the mountain, there are valleys where I used to run. One of them is called Kauaʻula. If you walked up into it before the sugar came, you would have heard me before you saw me: a sound like a crowd of people all talking at once, a rushing that filled the whole valley, cold and white over the stones. I came down out of the cloud, out of the moss and the fern, down through the rocks, past the little terraces where the families grew their taro, and at the bottom I spread out through the town of Lele in a hundred channels, filling the fishponds and the taro pools and the king’s pond in the middle, until I found my way to the sea. Where you are now. Right here.

Then men came with picks and shovels and dynamite, and with the laborers they brought, Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Portuguese, Hawaiian, and they climbed up into my valleys, and they cut tunnels into the rock above the places where I ran, and they built walls across my beds, and they turned me.

I want you to understand that I did not stop running. I can’t stop running. It isn’t in me. I only went where they told me. They sent me sideways along the mountain in ditches, in long dark tunnels where I ran blind for miles, in wooden flumes on stilts over the gulches. I went to the cane. Mile after mile of cane, tall and green and endlessly thirsty, and I gave myself to it, a ton of me for every pound of sugar, and the sugar went into ships, and the ships went to San Francisco, and the money went somewhere I never followed.

And in the town, the stream beds went dry. The taro pools cracked into plates of mud, curling up at the edges like old paper. The springs under the king’s pond weakened, and the pond went still and green and stinking, and then they filled it in with earth, and they put a ballpark on top of the king’s island, and the boys of the town played baseball over his bones.
That is a true thing. You can go and see it. Just a field.

The sugar left this side of the island at the end of the last century. Sugar could be grown cheaper elsewhere. The mill shut down. The cane was not replanted. You would think, wouldn’t you, that I would be let go then. That the walls would come down and the tunnels would be sealed and I would be allowed, after a hundred years, to go home the old way, down my own valley, through my own town.

Not all of me. Some of me, yes. People fought for it. The families who still wanted to grow taro the old way went to the water commission, and they went to the courts, again and again, year after year, and they argued that I belonged to everyone, that a river cannot be owned, that the law of this state says so in plain words. And sometimes they won, a little. A little more of me was let back into a stream bed. And sometimes they lost. But by then there were other thirsts. There was the new land being sold above the town, the house lots, the big lots sold as farms to people who don’t farm. There were the resorts up the coast with their lawns and their pools and their golf courses green as money. Somebody always needs me more than the stream bed does. That’s how it goes, in the end. Somebody always has a better reason.
Here’s what I want you to see, if you can.

On the day this happened, a man who managed some of the water on this side of the mountain wrote to the people in charge of me. He asked for permission to send more of me, out of the streams, into his reservoirs, so the reservoirs would be full if the fire came back. He was told to wait. He was told he needed to talk first to the farmers down below, the ones who used me for their taro, to make sure taking more would not hurt them. That was the law. It was a law that had been fought for, by those same taro farmers, for exactly the reason you might expect: because for a hundred years the big users had taken whatever they wanted without asking. His own water man, the one who knew the system, had gone to get his family out, and the others couldn’t be reached. Hours went by while the gates stayed shut.

Afterward the official who had asked him to wait was moved out of his job, and the people above him said it didn’t mean he’d done anything wrong. Afterward people asked whether a full reservoir would have saved anything. The man who’d asked for the water himself said nobody could know. His reservoirs weren’t even connected to the town’s fire hydrants. Others said that didn’t matter, a helicopter can dip a bucket in a reservoir. Others said the hydrants failed because the pipes melted in the burning houses and the water ran out of the broken pipes onto the ground, and the pressure dropped everywhere at once, and no reservoir on Earth could have fixed that. All of those things may be true together. That’s what you’ll have to decide.

I’ll tell you only what I know, which is what water knows. I was up there that day. In the tunnels. In the ditches.
