In the tanks and the pipes and the reservoirs, held behind gates, waiting for someone to sign a piece of paper. A few miles below me, the town that I used to run through, the town that used to be named for my shade, was on fire, and I could not get to it.
I’m not telling you this to make you angry. Anger is a fire too. I’m telling you because some day you might wonder why I’m salty. Why I taste of tears.
It isn’t only your tears. Some of it’s mine.
III. THE SEAWALL
11. Nobody Rang Anything Kanoe
At five o’clock I was sitting on the curb of the highway north of town with my phone in both hands, refreshing a screen that would not refresh.

There were hundreds of us. Cars pulled off on both shoulders, doors open, people standing on the hoods to see. People walking up the highway out of the smoke, out of Lahaina, with nothing. Black faces, black arms, eyes red as meat. A man in board shorts and nothing else, barefoot, the soles of his feet bleeding. A woman carrying a baby wrapped in a beach towel with a cartoon fish on it. They came out of the smoke in ones and twos and handfuls, and every time someone came, all of us who were waiting stood up at once, the way birds on a wire all lift together, and looked at their faces, and sat back down.
I asked every one of them. “Lahainaluna? Did you come from Lahainaluna? Did you see an old lady, white hair, a pencil in it? A boy, eight, no front teeth?”
Nobody had. Nobody had seen anything. “It came so fast,” they said. They all said that. “It came so fast. It was everywhere. It was in the trees. It was in the air.”

A man I knew a little from church, a big man with a voice like a truck in low gear, sat down next to me on the curb and put his face in his hands and said into them, “No siren. Kanoe. Nobody rang anything.”
“What?”

“The sirens.” He took his hands down and pointed, a soot-black finger, at a gray pole by the highway with the gray horn on top of it. There’s one every so often all along the coast. Tsunami sirens. They test them on the first working day of every month at eleven-forty-five in the morning, a long rising wail, so regular that people check their watches by it. “They never set them off. Not one. You know how I found out? My neighbor banged on my door. My neighbor. With a garden hose in his hand.”
I looked at the siren on the pole. Silent. Gray. Doing nothing in the wind.

Later we found out why. The man in charge of emergencies for the county said he didn’t sound them because the sirens are for tsunamis, and people here are trained, when the siren goes, to run uphill, mauka, away from the sea. And the fire was uphill. He said he was afraid people would run into the fire. That was his reason. Some people believe him. Some people don’t. He quit his job nine days later and said it was for health reasons. You decide.

I’ll tell you what I think, and then I’ll stop, because it doesn’t matter what I think. I think if that siren had gone off, my mother would have turned on the radio. She had a little transistor radio with batteries in the kitchen drawer, for hurricanes. She’d have turned it on and listened, because that’s what she did when the siren went. And she’d have heard the word fire. And she’d have had a few more minutes.
That’s all. A few minutes. That’s what a siren is. It doesn’t put anything out. It just tells you to start running a little sooner.

The phones didn’t work. Most of the cell towers on the west side had lost power the night before, and the ones with backup batteries had burned or run down. The landlines were down. The internet was down. There was no electricity anywhere in Lahaina, so there was no TV, and the radio station that might have said something wasn’t saying much, because nobody knew much, because nobody could reach anybody. The county was putting messages on its website and its social media. Nobody in Lahaina could see them. There was no alert that came to people’s phones with that loud screaming tone, the one they use for missing children and flash floods. Nobody sent it. Even if they had, most phones in the town had nothing to receive it with.
So the way you learned your town was burning was the way people learned it a thousand years ago. You smelled it. You saw it. Your neighbor banged on your door. Somebody ran down the street yelling.
That’s how they got out, the ones who got out. People. Not systems. People yelling at people.

When it got dark the sky over Lahaina turned the color of the inside of a mouth. The smoke above the town was lit from underneath, red and orange and a strange deep pink, and it pulsed, brightening and dimming, as if something under there were breathing. Every so often there’d be a bigger flare, a burst of light shooting up into the smoke, and then a few seconds later a sound would roll up the highway, a deep whump you felt in your stomach. People said that was propane tanks. Gas stations. Boats in the harbor. The harbor was burning, someone said. Every boat in it.
My son jumps off the harbor wall. Every day. I told you.

A fire truck came up the highway out of the smoke, slow, with people standing on the back of it, holding on, and its lights going, and everybody ran toward it, and I ran too. People were climbing down off it, black from head to foot, coughing, some of them wrapped in wet blankets. A firefighter jumped down with his face all white around his mask, like a raccoon in reverse, and started shouting at us to stay back, give them room, there’s a shelter at the civic center, go to the civic center, there’s water there.
I grabbed his arm. “Lahainaluna. Did you go up Lahainaluna?”
He looked at me. “Ma’am, there’s no Lahainaluna.”
I didn’t understand. “The road. Lahainaluna Road.”
“Ma’am,” he said again, gently, the way you’d talk to someone in a hospital, “it’s all gone up there. That’s where it started. It’s all gone.”
He pulled his arm away. Not hard. He had other people to tell.
I stood in the road with the fire truck’s lights going round and round, red, white, red, across my face, and I said out loud, to nobody, “They went to Auntie Rose’s. They went by the harbor.”
Then I remembered they hadn’t. At eleven they’d walked home. Keola wanted his ball.
12. The Wall Wes

I’m going to tell you this the way it was for me then. I owe that night that much. Afterward I learned a great many things, and where I’ve learned better since, I’ll say so, but I won’t fix what I thought. If I fixed it, it wouldn’t be what happened. It would be a report. So: the way it was.
We got four blocks north on Front Street. It took twenty minutes.

The street was solid with cars. Bumper to bumper, both lanes, all of them pointed north, all of them honking, none of them moving. People on foot were going faster than the cars, weaving between them, and every few seconds someone would give up on their car and get out and leave it there with the engine running and the door open and just start walking. The air was getting hotter. Not warm. Hot, the way it’s hot when you open an oven to check on something and lean too close. The ash coming down was bigger now, pieces of it the size of my thumbnail, some of them still glowing orange at the edges, drifting down through the brown dark like slow fireflies.

I had Theo by the hand. I’d tied my T-shirt over his mouth and nose, wet with one of the bottles of water. He was walking with his eyes shut half the time, letting me pull him. He wasn’t crying. That frightened me more than crying.

At the corner where I needed to turn to get to the parking lot, the street was blocked. A power pole was down across it, snapped off at the base, lying at an angle across the road with its wires hanging off it in loops, and there were men in hard hats and vests standing there waving people back. Utility crew. One of them was shouting, “Lines are down! Can’t go this way! Lines are down! Turn around!”
A man in a pickup leaned out of his window and screamed at him, “Where?! Turn around to where?!”
The utility guy just pointed. Back. South. Toward where we’d come from.

I didn’t know what to do. I’m a man who always knows what to do, and I stood on that corner with my son and I didn’t know which way was away. Behind us, south, the smoke was thick and red. Ahead of us, north, the street was blocked and the cars were stopped and there was fire now on the right too, on the mountain side, in the yards behind the buildings, I could see it through the gaps between them: palm trees going up like torches, one after another, the whole crown of a tree catching at once in a great roaring ball of orange and the dead fronds tearing off and flying away in the wind, burning, over our heads, over the street, toward the sea.

The wind was carrying the fire. That’s what I understood, standing there. It wasn’t coming down the hill the way a fire burns down a candle. It was being thrown. The wind was picking up burning pieces of everything, leaves, fronds, shingles, wood, and throwing them ahead, a block ahead, two blocks, onto roofs and into yards and into the open windows of cars, and wherever they landed a new fire started, and the new fires joined up. It was everywhere at once. There was no edge to it, no front line, no place where you could stand and say, this side is safe.
There was only one direction it wasn’t coming from.
I looked left, west, across Front Street, past the stopped cars, at the seawall and the water.

The seawall in Lahaina runs along the ocean side of Front Street for a long way. It isn’t high on the street side, waist height, a concrete wall with a flat top you can sit on, the kind of wall where in a normal week people sit and eat their ice cream and watch the sunset. On the ocean side it drops, six or eight feet, onto a slope of big black boulders, and then the water. It’s not a beach. It’s rocks and water. When we’d arrived on Thursday there’d been a couple sitting on that wall with their legs dangling, sharing a pineapple out of a plastic cup, and I’d thought: that’s the life.
There were people on it now. Climbing it. Going over.

I pulled Theo across the street, between the cars. A car door opened in front of us and I nearly ran him into it. Someone was screaming inside one of the cars, a long high sound, and I didn’t look. I’m sorry. I didn’t look. We got to the wall. Below us the rocks, slick and black, and the waves coming in on them white, hard, the wind blowing the spray off the tops, and floating in the water, holding onto the rocks, holding onto each other, people. Twenty. Thirty. In the dark, in the red light, their faces turned up toward the street, toward the fire.
Theo saw the water and pulled back so hard his hand came out of mine.
“No,” he said. “No. No. Dad. No.”
“Theo.”
“No.”

He was backing up, back toward the cars, toward the fire. I grabbed him. I got him by both arms. He fought me. He was nine and skinny and he fought me like an animal, kicking, twisting, his face screwed up, crying finally, crying and screaming, no no no, I can’t, I can’t, Dad, I can’t see under it, and behind him a car’s windshield cracked with the heat with a noise like a pistol shot, and I picked him up. I picked him up like a toddler, both arms round his body, his legs kicking against me, and I held him against my chest, and I said into his hair, “I’ve got you. I’ve got you. I’ve got you.”
And that’s when the old woman came.

She came out of the smoke from the north, from the side street, walking. Not running. She couldn’t run. She was small and round, wearing a muʻumuʻu [MOO-oo MOO-oo], a long loose flowered dress, and men’s rubber slippers, and she was holding a boy by the hand. The boy was pulling her, trying to make her go faster, and she was coming as fast as she could, which wasn’t fast. Her white hair had come loose and was blowing straight out sideways from her head in the wind like smoke itself. Her face was black with soot except for two clean lines down her cheeks where the tears had run.

The boy was the kid from the harbor wall. I knew him at once, even then, even black with ash. Skinny. All elbows. Hair sticking up at the back. He saw the water below the wall and he didn’t pull back. He pulled toward it.

The old woman looked at the wall. She looked at me, holding Theo, and at the people in the water, and then she looked down at her own legs, at her swollen ankles in the men’s slippers, and I saw her decide. I saw it. I’ve seen a thousand swimmers on a thousand starting blocks, and I know what a person’s face does in the half-second when they decide to go, and her face did the opposite.
“You,” she said to me. Her voice was hoarse from the smoke but it carried. It was a voice used to carrying. “You can swim?”
“Yes.”
“Good.” She pushed the boy forward, toward me, and the boy turned and looked up at her. “Take him.”
“Tūtū—“ the boy said.

“He swims,” she said to me, over the boy’s head, fast, hard, every word a separate stone. “He swims better than you. But he’s eight. You hold him. You don’t let go. You understand me? Whatever. You hold on.”
“Ma’am, come on, you come too, I’ll help you down—“

“I’m not going in there.” She almost laughed. It came out a cough. “Seventy-nine years I never went past my knees. Too late to start.” She looked at the boy. Her face did something I won’t describe. “Go with Uncle,” she said to him. “Go on. I’ll be right here. I’ll be right here on the wall.”
“Tūtū—“

“Go.” She put her hand on top of his head, flat, for just a second. Then she took it off and pushed his shoulder, toward me, toward the wall, toward the water, and she said the last thing. She said it to me. I’ve heard it every night since.
“Take my life,” she said. “Go on. Take my life.”

She didn’t look at me when she said it. She was looking at him. I’ve thought since that she was making sure of something, the way you check a knot before you trust your weight to it: his face, the hair standing up at the back, the gap where his front teeth had been. She looked at him the way you look at a thing for the last time when you know it is the last time and have decided not to make a fuss about it. Then she brought her hand back and folded it inside her other hand, in front of her, against the flowers of her dress, and held it there, as though it were still warm from the top of his head and she meant to keep the warmth for as long as it would last.

I didn’t understand her. I thought she was out of her mind with the smoke. I thought she meant, my life is over, save yourself, or something like that, something old women say in movies. I didn’t know, then, what the boy’s name meant.

There wasn’t time. The fire was in the building across the street now, the one with the T-shirt shop in it, the windows bursting out one after another, pop, pop, pop, and the heat came across the road like an open door.

I sat on the wall. I swung my legs over. Theo was locked round my neck now, his arms so tight I could hardly breathe, his face crushed into my shoulder, and he’d stopped fighting, he’d gone rigid, like a cat. I put my free hand down. The other boy took it. His hand was small and hot and very strong.
“Ready?” I said to him.
He nodded.
We went over. I slid down the rough face of the wall on my backside, Theo locked on my chest, the harbor boy sliding beside me with his hand in mine, and the rocks came up to meet us.
13. The Color of the Inside of a Mouth Kanoe

The civic center is a big gym and a parking lot on the highway between Kāʻanapali and Lahaina, outside the fire. By nine o’clock that night there were hundreds of people in it. They’d found generators. There were lights. There were cots coming in on trucks, and pallets of bottled water, and a church group from up the coast handing out rice and Spam musubi [moo-SOO-bee], which is a block of rice with a slice of fried Spam on top wrapped in seaweed, which is what you eat here when anything happens, birthday, funeral, end of the world.
I didn’t eat. I walked.

There was a whiteboard by the door where people were writing names. Somebody had started it and everybody had joined in, so it was already full, both sides, names written over names, in marker and in pen and in lipstick: LOOKING FOR and then a name and a street and a phone number that didn’t work. I found a space at the bottom corner and I wrote, small, because there was hardly room:
KEOLA, 8. TŪTŪ (79). LAHAINALUNA. — KANOE

I stood back and looked at it. It looked like nothing. It looked like a grocery list. I’d written my son’s name with a marker that was running out, so the K was dark and the A at the end was pale gray, nearly gone.
I went outside and walked across the parking lot to where you could see the town.

People had gathered at the edge of the lot, on a little rise of dry grass, and they were all standing very still, looking south. I stood with them. Nobody talked. I don’t think I’ve ever stood with so many people in so much silence.
Below us, Lahaina was burning.
I’m going to try to tell you what it looked like, because I promised myself that if I lived through it I’d tell it right, even the parts I don’t want to.

The whole town was a lake of fire. From the slope behind it to the sea, from end to end, every street, every block, glowing, red and orange and white, so bright that the smoke above it was lit up like the underside of a cloud at sunset, and the light came all the way up to where we were standing and painted our faces orange. You could see shapes inside the fire. The black skeletons of houses, standing up in the glow like the ribs of animals. Trees, like burning candles, a whole row of them along the road. A shape that I knew was the old church, the steeple, standing up straight and black against the brightness, and then, while I watched, slowly, leaning, and then gone.

And the sea. That was the worst. The sea in front of the town was red. The fire was reflected in it, the whole wide water from the seawall out to the reef glittering red and gold, moving, shining, so it looked as if the ocean were on fire too. And out in the harbor there were boats burning on the water, little ones and big ones, each one a separate fire floating on its own reflection, drifting slowly as their ropes burned through.
I stood there and thought: Keola jumps off that wall.
I stood there and thought: Mom doesn’t swim. Mom has never in her life gone past her knees.
I stood there and thought: they’re at Rose’s. They went back to Rose’s. Rose’s is by the harbor. The harbor is on fire.
I stood there and thought: no. They walked home. Keola wanted his ball.

I stood there and thought, and thought, in circles, the same three thoughts, round and round, like a dog chasing a smell, and the fire went on and on in front of me, and nobody on that hill said one word.
Around midnight a woman next to me, an older woman with a towel round her shoulders, started to sing.

Very quietly. Just under her breath at first. An old song, a mele [MEH-leh], which is the word for a Hawaiian song or chant, a song for a place. It was a song about Lahaina. About the breadfruit shade, and the sun, and the rain that comes down off the mountain in the night. I knew it. Every kid here learns it in school. One by one, the people standing on that hill joined in, very softly, until there were maybe fifty of us singing in the dark, in the orange light, looking down at our town burning, singing it a song about how beautiful it was.
I sang too. I didn’t decide to. I just did.

I’ll tell you something I’ve never told anyone. While I was singing, I had a feeling, very clear, very strong, like a hand on my back, that my mother was singing too. Somewhere down there. Not dead, not alive, just singing. I could almost hear her, her voice under all the others, that voice that could reach the end of the lane without trying.
That was the smoke, probably. We were all breathing a lot of smoke. It does things to you.
I’m telling you anyway. I promised to tell it right.
14. The Long Night Wes
The first thing the water did was hit us.

We went off the wall onto the rocks and the rocks were slick, black, covered in some kind of slime, and a wave came in as we landed and knocked my feet out from under me, and we went down together, all three of us, into the white churning water between the boulders. I went under. Theo went under with me, still locked round my neck. I felt his whole body jerk in panic. I got my feet on something and stood and came up and dragged him up with me, and he was choking, coughing salt water, screaming between coughs. And the other boy, the harbor boy, came up a few feet away, calm, his hair plastered flat, and swam to me in two strokes and grabbed the strap of my backpack, and held on.
Then the next wave came and we were all together against the rocks.
That’s how it was for a long time. I’m going to try to tell you how it was.

The water was waist deep where I stood, sometimes chest deep, when the waves came in. I had my back against a big rock at the base of the seawall, with the wall going up above us, and the rock was rough and it scraped my back every time a wave pushed me into it. I had Theo in front of me, his arms round my neck, his legs round my waist. I had the harbor boy on my left side, holding my backpack strap, floating easy, his chin just above the water. Every time a wave came he rose with it like a cork and came down and was still there.

The waves were the hard part. The wind was blowing off the land, out to sea, so you’d think the waves would be small, but they weren’t. They came in big and crooked, wild, as if the whole ocean were confused, and they rolled in and broke over us and pushed us into the rocks, and then sucked out and tried to drag us off the rocks and out into the dark, and we’d hang on, and they’d come in again. Every wave, I braced. Every wave, I counted. A coach counts. One, two, here it comes, hold. Hold. Three, four, five, breathe. I counted waves the way I count laps, out loud sometimes, so the boys could hear me. A hundred waves. Two hundred. I lost count somewhere after three hundred and started again.
Above us was the fire.

Picture it from where I was. I was looking up from the bottom of a wall, from the water, at the sky. The sky was gone. There was no sky. There was a ceiling of smoke, low, rolling, black and brown and lit from below in red, and it was moving, fast, out over the water above us, going out to sea, and out of it, all the time, coming down, was fire. Embers. Sparks. Burning things. Pieces of palm frond, still flaming, came spinning down out of the dark and hit the water around us and hissed and went out. Pieces of paper. Pieces of roof. Something that I think was part of a beach umbrella came down burning like a parachute and landed on the rocks ten feet from us and burned there for a long time.

The heat came over the wall in waves, like the water came. You could feel it on the top of your head, on your face if you looked up. We kept our heads down. Every so often, when a really bad gust came, a gust full of embers, I’d say, “Under!” and we’d all three duck our heads under the water for as long as we could, and I’d feel the hot rain of sparks on the back of my neck through the water, and we’d come up gasping.

Theo couldn’t go under. Not by himself. The first time I said “Under!” he just clung to me and screamed, and a piece of burning something landed on his shoulder and I slapped it off. After that I did it for him. I’d say “Breathe, bud, hold it, hold it,” and I’d wait till he took a breath, and I’d put my hand over his face and take him down with me. Two seconds. Three. Up. He’d come up choking and screaming and I’d say, “Good, good, that’s good, you did it,” the way I’d say it to a six-year-old at the Y.
The harbor boy went under by himself every time. He didn’t need to be told. He’d see a gust coming before I did and duck, quick, neat, and come up, wipe his face with one hand, and hold on.
The smoke was the thing that got into me.

It came down on the water in long rolling banks, sometimes so thick I couldn’t see the boys a foot from my face, couldn’t see my own hand. It got in your throat and your chest and burned like breathing pepper. Down at the water it was a little better, the air right at the surface, so we kept our faces low. But it got in anyway. All night it got in. My head started to ache, a deep, slow, throbbing ache behind my eyes. My eyes stopped working right. Everything got blurry and doubled and stung so bad I could hardly keep them open. And my thinking slowed. It went thick and strange, like thinking underwater.

I know now what that was. The smoke from a fire is full of a gas called carbon monoxide, which you can’t see or smell, and which gets into your blood and takes the place of oxygen. A little of it gives you a headache. More makes you confused, slow, dreamy, sleepy. More than that makes you see things. More than that, and you lie down and don’t get up. People who breathe smoke for hours in a fire, I’ve since read, often remember the night afterward in pieces, out of order, full of things that couldn’t have been there.
So some of what I’m about to say couldn’t have been there.
I’ll say it anyway.
At some point, I don’t know when, I don’t know what hour, the water started to get cold.

You’d think it couldn’t. It’s Hawaii. The water’s warm as a bath. But if you stand in a bath for three hours, four hours, with the wind blowing over your wet head and shoulders, it takes the heat out of you a little at a time, and doesn’t give it back. I started to shake. My teeth went. I could feel Theo shaking against me, his whole little body rattling like a machine.

And the explosions. Cars, along Front Street, right above us. A car’s gas tank goes up with a flat, thudding bang that you feel in your chest more than hear, and then a whoosh, and a wave of heat, and burning pieces of car come over the wall. They went off every few minutes, all down the street, some close, some far. Every time one went off close, the boys flinched against me.
Here is the part I have to tell carefully.

Sometime after it was fully dark, a car went up just along from us. On the street above the wall, maybe twenty feet down. I don’t know what was in it. The bang wasn’t a bang. It was a blow, like being hit in the face with a door. A sheet of white fire came out over the top of the wall, and a wave came in at the same time, a big one, the biggest yet, and I don’t know which hit us first. I know that I went under. I know that I was thrown off the rock, pushed along the bottom, rolled over, my shoulder slammed into something hard, my head hit something, and I couldn’t tell which way was up. Everything was black and roaring and full of bubbles. My arms were empty.
My arms were empty.

I have held children in water for twenty years. A child in water weighs almost nothing. Five pounds, maybe, of a sixty-pound boy; the sea takes the rest. You stop feeling it after a while. It becomes part of your arms, the way a watch becomes part of your wrist, and you only know it’s there when it’s gone. That’s how I knew. Not by looking. I couldn’t see anything. By the lightness. My arms came up through the black water too fast, too easy, as if a rope had been cut, and that lightness was the worst thing I have ever felt in my life, worse than the heat, worse than the smoke. Five pounds. About what his mother weighed in the bag. My arms knew before I did.

I came up. I don’t know how. I was a few yards out from where we’d been, in deeper water, and I couldn’t touch bottom, and I couldn’t see. Smoke on the water, thick, and the red light through it, and the waves, and I was turning, turning in the water, screaming his name.
“THEO! THEO!”
Nothing. Waves. Smoke.
“THEO!”

And then something bumped against my chest in the dark, small, kicking, coughing. A boy. I grabbed him. I got my arms round him and pulled him into me and he came, he grabbed my neck, he held on, coughing, retching up seawater against my shoulder, his heart going like a hummingbird against mine.
“I’ve got you,” I said. “I’ve got you. I’ve got you, bud. I’ve got you.”
I swam us back to the wall. I don’t know how I found it. I found it. I got my back against a rock again and my feet on the bottom.
Then I remembered the other one.
“The other boy,” I said, out loud, to the dark. “The other boy.” I had his grandmother’s voice in my ear: You hold him. You don’t let go. Whatever.

I yelled. I didn’t know his name. Did I? Had she said it? I couldn’t remember. The smoke. I yelled “HEY! KID! HEY!” into the dark and the smoke and the red light, over and over, and I waited, and there was nothing but the waves and the fire and, far down the wall, other people in the water, yelling other names.
And this is what I thought, exactly, because it’s the thing I’ll answer for, whatever there is to answer to.

I thought: he swims. She said it. He swims better than you. I saw him backflip off the harbor wall. I saw him swim like a seal. He’s fine. He’s somewhere down the wall with the others, holding on. He can swim. He’ll be fine. He’s the one who’ll be fine.
I held my son against my chest and I told myself that, and I believed it, because I needed to, and because I had my son.
The hours after that I can only give you in pieces.

The boy in my arms stopped shaking. That’s the first piece. I don’t know how long after. Maybe an hour. He’d been rigid, his arms locked round my neck, and then at some point I felt him go soft. I was terrified, I thought he’d passed out, and I pulled his head back to look at him. And he was awake. His eyes were open, looking at me, black face, white eyes. And he let go of my neck. He let go, and lay back, and put his ears in the water, and floated. Just like I’d taught him a hundred times when he was four. Arms out. Chin up. Ears under. Giving the water his weight. He lay there in the black and red water, held only by my hand flat under the small of his back, floating, calm, breathing slow, looking up at the burning sky.

I started to cry. I’m not ashamed of it. I stood there against that rock with my hand under my son’s back and cried like a child, because he was floating. Because after two years he’d finally done it, he’d finally trusted the water. Here. Tonight. In the middle of hell. Claire, I said. Claire, look. He’s floating. He’s doing it.

I kept my hand where it was, flat under his back. With a kid who has just learned, you leave it there longer than you need to, so they never feel the moment it goes. Above us the smoke went over, red and black, and pieces of the town came down burning and hissed out on the water a few feet off, and he watched them fall the way you’d watch snow from a window. His breath went in and out, slow. I could feel it through my palm, the small rise of his ribs, the water lifting him a little higher on every breath in and letting him down on every breath out. Fifteen breaths a minute. Fourteen. Twelve. I counted them. I would have counted them all night.
That’s the second piece. Here’s the third.
At some point, the boy in my arms called me Uncle.

He said, quiet, in a voice that sounded like it came from far off, “Uncle, my Tūtū stay on the wall?” There was a little whistle in it, at the edges of the words. I thought it was his teeth chattering.

And I laughed. God help me, I laughed. I thought he was remembering the kid from the harbor, the one who’d called me Uncle, the one who’d come into the water with us. I thought the smoke had him mixed up, the way it had me mixed up. I said, “We’ll find her, bud. Don’t worry. We’ll find everybody.”

And later, another time, he said a word I didn’t know. He was floating with his face to the sky and he said, very soft, almost singing, “Kai [KYE].” Just that. A word I didn’t know. “Kai.” I thought it was a name. I thought maybe he was saying Claire, the way he used to say it when he was two and couldn’t get his mouth round it, Kai, Kai. I said, “She’s here, bud. She’s right here.” And I believed that too.
The fourth piece is the one I can’t explain.
Sometime in the deepest part of the night, the smoke lifted off the water for a while, and I looked up, and Lahaina wasn’t burning anymore.

It was gone. The fire was gone. The burning buildings were gone, and the cars, and Front Street. And in their place, under the red sky, there was a different town. There were trees. Enormous, dark, round-headed trees, hundreds of them, breadfruit, I know now, though I didn’t know the word then, standing in groves with paths between them. And there was water everywhere. Running water. I could hear it. Streams coming down out of the dark from the mountain, dozens of them, pouring through the town in channels lined with stone, glittering red in the firelight. And pools, square pools stepping down the slope one after another, flooded and shining like mirrors, with green leaves standing up out of them, big leaves shaped like hearts. And right there, close, just over where the wall had been, there was a wide pond, still and black, and in the middle of the pond a small island, with a low house on it made of grass, and torches burning in front of the house, and somebody standing in the doorway.
I could hear the water running. That’s what I remember most. The whole town full of the sound of running water, like the town itself was laughing.
And I could hear, on the wall above me, very clear, an old woman singing.

I don’t know the words. It wasn’t English. It was slow, and it went up and down like the waves, and it didn’t stop. It just went on and on, a voice used to carrying, singing into the fire. Singing to somebody.

I lay back against the rock with my son floating under my hand, and I listened to that woman singing, and I listened to the water running through the old town, and for a while, I don’t know how long, I wasn’t afraid of anything.
Then the smoke came back down, and the town was burning again, and the singing had stopped.
The last piece is this.

My backpack had torn. I didn’t know when. Somewhere in the rocks, in the blast, in the wave. The strap that the harbor boy had been holding had ripped half away from the bag, and the bag had a long gash down the side, and everything in it was gone, the wallet, the phone, the water bottles, the inhaler. All of it gone into the dark.
I noticed it near the end. I put my hand back to feel for the inhaler, because the boy’s breathing had gone rough, and the bag was empty, just a torn wet sack hanging off my shoulder.

And around us in the water, from the bang onward, there had been a strange pale cloudiness. I didn’t understand it. I thought it was ash from the fire. A soft gray haze in the water, just under the surface, drifting, catching the red light. It came and went with the waves. It was there on my arms and on the boy’s chest when I looked. A fine pale dust, like flour. Like the finest sand.
I put my hand in it and watched it slide off my fingers and I thought: ash. The town. That’s the town.
It wasn’t only the town.
15. Dawn Kanoe

The sun came up on the ninth of August the way it does every morning in Lahaina: from behind the mountain, slow, the sky over the ridge going gray, then pale gold, then a thin bright line along the top of the mountain like the edge of a knife.
Except the mountain was black.

I’d fallen asleep on the grass at the edge of the parking lot, sitting up, with my knees pulled to my chin, and I woke up with the sun coming over the ridge and the first thing I saw was that the mountain behind Lahaina, the slope I had looked at every day of my life, was black from the town halfway to the clouds. Black and smoking. Gray smoke drifting up off it in a thousand thin threads, like steam off a cup.

And below it, where the town had been, there was smoke too. Not fire anymore, mostly. A gray low haze, flat, lying over everything, so you couldn’t see what was under it. Here and there, through the haze, a little orange glow still, a few spots still burning. A thin column going up from where the harbor was. The banyan, I thought. I looked for the dark green bump of the banyan tree. I couldn’t find it. I couldn’t find anything. There was nothing to find it against.
People were waking up around me on the grass. Nobody said anything. We stood up, one at a time, and looked.
All that morning they came out. Buses, trucks, ambulances, cars, people walking. All morning I stood at the entrance to the civic center and watched every face.

I want to tell you about the faces. Most of them were not hurt, not in a way you could see. They were just black, from the smoke, every one of them, hair and skin and clothes, all the same color, as if the fire had made them all one family. Their eyes were red. Some of them had burns, on their arms, on their backs, red and wet, and they went straight to the medical tent, where a nurse from the hospital in Wailuku, who hadn’t slept since the day before, was cleaning burns. A lot of them were wet. Soaked. Seawater dried white on their clothes in salt lines. People said that a lot of them had been in the ocean. All night. Along the seawall. That the firefighters had got some of them out after midnight and the rest after it got light. That surfers had paddled in through the reef on their boards in the dark and taken the little kids first.
I asked every one. “Did you see an old lady, white hair? Was there a boy? Eight. No front teeth. A swimmer.”
One woman, very young, with a baby, looked at me a long time. “There was a lot of boys,” she said. “In the water. I don’t know. I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”

Everyone was sorry. I was sorry. I was sorry for everything. I was sorry I went to work. I was sorry I didn’t wake him. I was sorry about the dishes and the loose nail in the roof and every time I’d shouted at him to get off the harbor wall. I was sorry I hadn’t charged my phone a third time.
At about nine I went back inside the gym to look at the whiteboard. Somebody had written underneath my message, in blue: TŪTŪ AND
KEOLA — SAW THEM LAHAINALUNA 3PM WALKING MAKAI. —
D. Makai. Toward the sea.

I stood and read it ten times. Walking toward the sea. At three. That was all. Somebody named D. had seen them walking down the hill toward the sea, toward Front Street, at three o’clock in the afternoon. I didn’t know any D. I didn’t care. I wanted to find D. and hold their face in my hands and kiss them.
Toward the sea. Not toward the fire. Toward the sea.
Tūtū, you smart old woman. You smart, smart old woman.

I was still standing there, with my fingers on the blue letters as if I could read more out of them by touch, when I heard someone calling my name across the gym. A man’s voice. Loud. Calling it over and over, the way you call someone in a crowd when you’ve got something you can’t hold much longer.
“Kanoe! Kanoe! Anybody seen Kanoe from Lahainaluna?! Kanoe!”
16. I Got Him Wes
The boards came out of the dark sometime after midnight.

I didn’t see them at first. I heard them. Voices, out on the water, behind us, beyond the reef, men shouting to each other in a mix of English and something else, and then a splashing, steady, rhythmic, the sound of arms paddling hard. And then, out of the smoke, low on the water, there they were. Three men on surfboards, lying flat on their stomachs, paddling in through the gap in the reef toward the wall, toward us, toward all the people in the water. They had headlamps on, little white lights bobbing in the smoke.
People along the wall started shouting. “Here! Here! Over here! Kids! There’s kids!”

The first board came straight for us. A big man, older, heavy in the shoulders, lying on a long board, his headlamp swinging. He came in close, slid off the board into the water beside me, held the board steady with one hand. His face was black like everybody’s. His eyes were white.
“Keiki [KAY-kee] first,” he said. Keiki, I know now, means children. “Brah. Give me the boy. I take him out to the boat. Got one boat outside the reef. Give him.”
I didn’t want to let go. I had held him all night. I had promised. You don’t let go. Whatever.
“Careful with him,” I said. “That’s Theo. That’s my Theo. You’re okay, bud. You’re okay.”
“It’s okay,” the man said. “Brah. It’s okay. I got him.”

I lifted the boy off my chest. He was floating, still, half asleep. I lifted him up and the man took him under the arms and slid him onto the front of the surfboard, on his stomach, and put one big hand flat on his back to hold him there.
The man looked at the boy’s face in the light of the headlamp. And something happened in the man’s face. I saw it even through the black and the smoke. It went still, and then it broke open.
“Eh,” he said, very soft. “Eh.” Then louder, to the other boards, to the dark, his voice cracking: “I got him! I got him! I got him!”
I thought he meant: I’ve got him. Safe. Like you’d say it to a parent. I thought that’s what everybody said.
“Thank you,” I said. “Thank you. Thank you.” I couldn’t stop saying it.

The boy turned his head on the board and looked back at me. Black face. White eyes. In the headlamp light. He looked at me for a long moment, the way a child looks at a stranger, and he lifted one hand off the board, a little, and he said:
“Bye, Uncle.”

Then the man was paddling, kicking, pushing the board out through the waves toward the gap in the reef and the boat beyond it, and the headlamp went bobbing away into the smoke, smaller, smaller, and was gone.

Bye, Uncle. I stood there in the water against the rock and I smiled, I swear to you, I smiled, because I thought: he’s still doing it. He’s still mixed up, still playing the harbor kid. That’s my funny boy. That’s my brave, funny boy.

The firefighters came down the wall at about one-thirty in the morning. I learned the time later. Ladders, ropes, headlamps, big men in yellow coats, reaching down, pulling people up one by one. Two of them pulled me up. I couldn’t climb. My legs wouldn’t work. They’d been in the water nine hours and they’d forgotten what they were for. The firefighters lifted me over the top of the wall like a sack of something and laid me on the street.

Along the top of the wall, in the smoke, there were people sitting who didn’t get up when the firefighters passed them. I saw them the way you see furniture in a dark room, a shape, and then another shape. Nobody went to them. I didn’t look closer. I’ve had to live with that too, so I’ll say it plainly: I didn’t look.

The street was burning. Still. Not everywhere now, but in patches, the cars along the curb burned down to black frames, glowing red in their wheel wells, the buildings across the road just walls now, empty windows full of orange light. The heat on my face. The smell, which I won’t describe, because somebody reading this has children, and I don’t want you to have to know it.

They carried me to a fire truck and put me on the back of it with other people from the water. Somebody put a blanket on me. Somebody gave me a bottle of water and I couldn’t hold it, my hands were shaking too much, so they held it for me while I drank.
“My son,” I said. “My son. A man took him on a surfboard. To a boat.”
“Okay,” said the firefighter. “Okay. They took a bunch of kids out to the boats. They’ll bring them in by boat up the coast and take them to the shelter. You’ll find him. Okay? You’ll find him.”
“He’s nine. Theo. Curly hair.”
“Okay. You’ll find him. Drink your water.”

The truck started to move. Slowly, around burned cars, through smoke, along what had been Front Street, past what had been the banyan tree, which I couldn’t see, which I couldn’t see anything of. People on the back of the truck were crying, or quiet, or coughing. I was smiling. I know how that sounds. I was lying on the back of a fire truck going through the ruins of a town where I didn’t know how many people had died and I had my face turned up to the smoke, and I was smiling, because my son had floated. Because he had done it. Because he was on a boat, outside the reef, safe, and in a few hours I’d find him in some shelter wrapped in a blanket and I’d pick him up and tell him, You floated, bud. You floated all night. Your mom saw.
I closed my eyes. I was so tired. I’d been counting for nine hours.
I stopped counting.
Said at the Seawall
I’ll tell you what I saw when they came over the wall. I saw all of it. I’m the only one who did.

I saw them come over the wall. Forty of them, more or less, along that stretch of stone, and others in other places, at the harbor, on the beach to the north, in the shallows by the boat ramp. They came down onto my rocks out of the burning street, the way animals come down to a river when the forest is on fire. They didn’t think about it. Something older than thinking told them: the water. Go to the water. Even the ones who were afraid of me came. Even the ones who’d never gone past their knees.
I held them.

I want you to know I tried. I’m not a gentle thing. I’ve thrown boats onto the rocks and taken whole beaches away in a night. But I tried. I made myself warm for them, as warm as I could for as long as I could. I lifted them when the waves came, so they wouldn’t be dragged along the bottom. I put my body between them and the sky when the burning things came down. I hid their faces in me, in my dark, again and again, and the embers hissed against my skin and went out, and the ones I was hiding came up again breathing.

There was a woman who held on to a boat’s anchor rope all night so the waves wouldn’t take her. There was a family of five on a piece of plywood. There was a toddler holding on to the neck of a stranger. There was a boy, nineteen, who told his mother and his little brother that if it came to it he would swim them to the next town at first light, and meant it. There was an old man who couldn’t bear it anymore and climbed back up over the wall into the street. There were people calling for each other in the dark, all night, names going up into the smoke and nobody answering. I heard all of them. I kept all the names.
Here is what I couldn’t do.

I couldn’t go up the wall. That’s all. Twenty feet. The width of a street. The fire was right there, right above me, burning the town that had once been named for my shade, burning the houses built on the beds where I used to run, and I lay at the bottom of the wall all night with my arms full of people and I could not climb twenty feet to put it out.

Do you understand? I’m not asking you to forgive anyone. I don’t know who to forgive, and neither do you. I’m only asking you to understand how it looked from down here. On the land above me, hydrants opened and nothing came out, or a little came out and then nothing, because the pipes were melting in the burning houses and I was pouring out of the broken ends onto the ground, wasted, running away under the floors. Up in the mountain I was sitting in tunnels and tanks behind closed gates. And down here, I was everywhere. I was a whole ocean, right there, a few steps away. And no one could carry me up.

In the harbor the boats burned on top of me. You could see the fire on them and the fire under them, their reflections, two flames for each boat, one reaching up and one reaching down, like hands trying to touch through glass. They burned to their waterlines, and then I took them. One by one. They came down to me slowly, hissing, and lay on my floor, and I hold them now, all of them, in the dark under the harbor, with the old anchors and the whalers’ bottles and the bones of the first canoes.
Toward the middle of the night, the old woman on the wall began to sing.

She had sat down on top of the wall, right above the place where the man was holding the boys. She’d sat there since the start, with her slippers off and her bare feet hanging over the edge, over me. I don’t think she could have gone anywhere else. Her legs were done. And sometime in the night, when the smoke was very bad and the heat was coming over the street in waves, she began to sing. Old words. A song for this place, a song her grandmother sang to her, about the shade of the breadfruit and the streams running down at night. She sang it out over me, slow, up and down. She sang it the whole way through, and then she started again from the beginning. And sometime after that, I don’t know when, she stopped.

She wasn’t singing to the fire. I want you to know that. She wasn’t singing to God, or to her daughter, or to herself. She was singing down. Down over the edge of the wall, into the dark, into the water, where she couldn’t see anymore, to someone she’d given away.
I carried every word of it. I carried it down into me, every note, and kept it. I have it now.
I’ll give it to you later. When you need it.
IV. UNACCOUNTED
17. Another Name Kanoe
It was Bully calling my name.

That isn’t his real name. Nobody knows his real name, or nobody uses it. He lived three houses down from us on the lane, a big heavy man of sixty with a gray ponytail and hands like baseball gloves, and he’d taught half the kids on our street to surf, including me, a long time ago, and including my son. He had a dog called Poi [POY], after the soft purple paste we make from taro root, and a truck that didn’t run. He used to sit on his lanai in the evenings with a beer and holler at Tūtū across and down the lane about the news, and she’d holler back, and that was their friendship, forty years of hollering.

He was standing in the middle of the gym, black from head to foot, in a pair of wet board shorts and nothing else, with his ponytail burned half off and a blanket round his shoulders, and in his arms he was holding my son.

I don’t remember crossing the gym. I remember Keola’s face. I remember that it turned toward my voice, and that his eyes found me, and that he didn’t say anything. He didn’t cry or shout or reach for me. He just looked at me, the way you look at something from very far away, from the other end of a long tunnel. Then Bully put him down and he walked to me, slowly, like an old man, and he put his arms round my waist and his face against my stomach, and held on.

I got down on my knees on the floor of that gym and held him. I held him so hard. He smelled of smoke and salt and something else, something burned, and his skin was cold, cold right through, even in that hot gym, and he was shaking, a little shaking all over, like a motor. His hair was stiff with salt. His back was scraped raw in long lines. He didn’t make a sound.
“Baby,” I said. “Baby, baby, baby.” That’s all I could say. I said it into his hair, a hundred times. “Baby. Baby. Mama’s here. Baby.”

I want to say I thought something. I didn’t. There was no room in me for thinking. There was his weight, which I knew. The back of his neck under my hand, which I knew. The little bump of bone at the top of his spine, the one I used to rub when he couldn’t sleep. I went over him with my hands the way you go through a house after a storm, room by room, checking. Head. Ears. Shoulders. Arms. Fingers, all ten. I counted them. I’m not a counter. I counted them twice. Then I put my nose in his hair, under the salt and the smoke, looking for the smell of him, the real one. It took a long time. It was there.
He didn’t say anything.
Bully sat down on a cot beside us, heavy, and put his face in his huge hands, and his shoulders went up and down.

When he could talk he told me. He’d gone out on his board after midnight, him and two of the young guys who surf the break off the harbor, because they’d heard there were people in the water along the seawall, and somebody had a boat outside the reef that couldn’t get in over the rocks. So the surfers went in. Lay on their boards and paddled in through the gap in the reef, in the dark, in the smoke, with embers coming down, with the fire right there, and started bringing people out. Kids first. Bully took three kids out. He’d go in, take a kid on the front of his board, paddle him out to the boat, hand him up, go back in for another. The third time he went in, there was a man against the wall holding a boy, and the man gave him the boy, and Bully put his light on the boy’s face, and it was Keola.

“I didn’t know,” Bully said. “Kanoe, I didn’t know. I just saw his face. I just saw, eh, that’s Kanoe’s boy. That’s Tūtū’s boy.” He wiped his face with the back of his wrist and left a clean stripe. “I yelled. I was yelling I got him, I got him. I was so happy, Kanoe. I was so happy.”
“Where was Mom? Was Mom there?”
He looked at me. He looked down at his hands.
“I didn’t see Tūtū,” he said. “There was people on the wall. On the top. Some of them. I didn’t—it was dark, it was smoke, I didn’t look up. I was looking at the water. I’m sorry. I didn’t look up.”
I held my son. I didn’t ask again. I knew Bully would have told me if there was anything to tell.
“Who was the man?” I said. “Holding him. Who was he?”

“Haole [HOW-leh].” Haole is what we call white people here. It can be rude. It can just be a description. In Bully’s mouth that morning it was just a description, a tired one. “Tourist, I think. Strong. Big shoulders. He was holding Keola like this—“ Bully made a shape with his arms, a cradle, one big hand flat. “All night, I think. He was crying. He kept saying thank you. Thank you, thank you.” Bully stopped. Something was bothering him. I could see it in his face. “Kanoe. One thing. The man was calling him something. When I took him.”
“Calling him what?”

“Another name. Not Keola. He kept saying it. Like the man thought—“ Bully stopped again. He looked at my son with his face against my stomach. “He kept saying Theo. Theo, Theo, you’re okay, bud. Like that. Like Keola was his.”

I didn’t understand, then, what it meant. I thought the man had been out of his mind with smoke, the way everybody had been out of their minds. I thought, he probably had a boy called Theo, and he held my son all night, in the fire, in the water, and kept him alive, and called him by his own boy’s name to keep himself going. I thought: God bless him. I thought: I’ll find him one day and I’ll cook for him for the rest of his life.
I didn’t think about the other boy. About where Theo was, if there was a Theo.
That came later. That came that evening, when the man walked into the gym.
18. Bye, Uncle Wes
I woke up in a hospital bed in Wailuku with a tube in my nose and a needle in my arm and a nurse leaning over me saying my name.

It was the afternoon of the ninth. I’d been brought in sometime in the early morning with smoke in my lungs and my body temperature low, and they’d given me oxygen and warm fluids and let me sleep. The nurse was young and tired and kind. Her name tag had a long Hawaiian name on it that my eyes, still stinging from the smoke, couldn’t read.
“Mr. Talbert? You’re in the hospital. You’re okay. You breathed in a lot of smoke. You’re going to be okay.”
“My son.”
“Okay.”
“My son. Theo. Nine. Surfers took him to a boat. Where is he?”
She looked at the chart. She looked at me. “I don’t know, sir. I’ll find out. They’ve got lists at the shelters. I’ll call.”

She called. I heard her in the hall, on a phone, saying Talbert, Theo, nine, and spelling it, and then waiting, and then saying okay, and then okay, and then nothing. She came back in and said the lists weren’t complete yet, a lot of the children who’d been brought out of the water were at the shelter at the civic center on the west side, and that as soon as I could stand up, someone would drive me.

I stood up. I pulled out the needle myself. The nurse said a word I won’t repeat and put a cotton ball on my arm and taped it, and then, because she was kind, she found me a T-shirt and a pair of shorts from a donation box and a Red Cross volunteer with a pass who was driving supplies out to the west side.

The civic center was a big gym full of cots and smoke-smell and quiet. That’s what I remember: how quiet it was. Hundreds of people and hardly a sound. People sitting on cots. People lying on cots with their arms over their eyes. Kids asleep in piles like puppies. A long whiteboard by the door covered in names. Volunteers going up and down the rows with water and rice.
I went down the rows. I looked at every child. Not him. Not him. Not him.
And then, at the end of the third row, against the far wall, there was a woman sitting on a cot, Hawaiian, about my age, in a hotel housekeeping uniform with the shirt-tail out, gray-black with ash.

She had a boy in her lap. A boy, eight or nine, curled up against her, his face in her neck, his legs folded up. She was rocking him, very slightly, forward and back. Next to her on the cot sat an enormous man with a burned-off gray ponytail, the man from the surfboard, still in his board shorts.
The boy’s back was scraped in long raw lines. His hair stood up at the back like a duck’s tail.
I stopped walking.
He must have felt me looking, the way children do. He turned his head on his mother’s shoulder and looked across the gym at me. Dark eyes in a brown face, washed clean now. Both front teeth missing.
He looked at me for a long time. Then he lifted one hand off his mother’s shoulder, a little, the way he had from the surfboard.
“Uncle,” he said.
I’m going to tell you what happened inside me, and then I’m going to stop for a while, and you’ll forgive me.

I understood everything at once. Not one thing after another. All of it, in a single piece, the whole night, the way you suddenly see the shape of a pool from the high board, the whole thing laid out at once in a single glance.

The bang. The wave. My arms empty. The boy who bumped into my chest in the dark, small, kicking, coughing. The boy who went soft, and lay back, and floated, calm, with his ears in the water, looking at the fire. He finally trusts the water. The boy who said Uncle, my Tūtū stay on the wall? The boy who said Kai. The boy who said Bye, Uncle.
The boy who swam better than me.
The boy whose name I hadn’t known.

And somewhere back there in the black water by the rocks, after the bang, while I was screaming Theo! Theo!, and grabbing the first body that bumped into me, and swimming back to the wall, and holding on, and holding on, and telling myself the other boy would be fine, because the other boy could swim, the other boy was the one who’d be fine, somewhere back there my son, who could not swim, who could not put his face in, who was afraid of what was under it, had been alone in the dark.
All night. Twenty feet away. Ten. Five. I’ll never know.
I’d held the wrong boy.
I’d held the wrong boy all night, and cried over him, and told my dead wife to look at him, and smiled when he waved goodbye to me.

I stood in the middle of that gym and did what I always do. I measured. Waist deep at the rock. Chest deep where the wave threw me. Past the end of the rocks, more than I could touch, and then the reef, and then the channel, and then the blue that goes down. The first thing they teach you at every lifeguard training is that drowning is quiet. It doesn’t splash. It doesn’t shout. It looks like nothing. I’d been shouting his name into the dark, and he’d have been somewhere in that dark, quiet, and I’d have been listening for the wrong sound. I did the sums standing there with my hands open at my sides, and they came out the same every time, and there was nobody to hand them to.
The woman was looking at me now. Over the boy’s head. She’d seen her son speak to me, and she’d seen my face, and she was putting it together, the way I’d put it together, a second behind me.
The big man stood up off the cot. “That’s him,” he said to her quietly. “That’s the guy. That’s the guy was holding him.”

She looked at me. I’ll never forget her face. It was full of the most complicated thing I’ve ever seen on a human face: gratitude and horror and pity and grief, all at once, all of it real, none of it canceling the others out.
“You,” she said. “You held my son.”
I said, “Where’s mine?”

I said it to her as if she would know. As if she’d have him. As if it were a mix-up at the coat check, and she’d reach behind the cot and bring out the right one, a little thin boy with his mother’s dark curls, and say Sorry, here you go.
She didn’t say anything. She couldn’t. She just held her boy tighter and looked at me with that face.

I turned around. I walked out. I don’t remember walking out. I remember the parking lot, the hot asphalt, the sky still brown with smoke, and that I was walking south, along the highway, toward the town, toward the seawall, toward the water, and that it was a long way, and that somebody, a policeman, a young one with red eyes, stopped me at the roadblock and put his hand up flat, and said, “Sir, nobody’s going in,” and I said, “My son is in there,” and he said, “I’m sorry,” and I said, “My son is nine,” and he said, “Sir, I’ve got a kid too,” and I sat down in the middle of the highway, and I didn’t get up for a long time.
19. The List Kanoe
In the days after, there was a list.

You might have heard about it. For a while, the whole world heard about it. It was a list of the people nobody could find. The unaccounted for, they called them, which is a phrase that sounds like bookkeeping, like a column of numbers that won’t add up. At the start it was more than a thousand names. A thousand people somebody had reported missing and nobody had found. Then, day by day, people were found: in shelters, at cousins’ houses on the other side of the island, on planes to Honolulu, in hospitals, asleep on a friend’s couch with a dead phone. Their names came off the list. And other names came off for the other reason.

I went to the place where they took the swabs. That’s how they found out who the dead were, the ones the fire hadn’t left enough of to know by their faces. They took DNA. They scraped the inside of your cheek with a long cotton swab, like a giant Q-tip, gently, both sides, and they put the swab in a little tube with a label, and they used it to match you against what they found. A family member gives a swab, and if your family member is among the dead, the swab will say so. It takes weeks. You go home and you wait.
I gave my swab for my mother.

A woman in a white mask and a blue paper gown did it. She was very kind. She said open, please, and this won’t hurt, and thank you, and when it was done she put her gloved hand on my shoulder for a second and didn’t say anything. There was a line of people behind me. A long line. Old people, young people, people holding photos. A man in front of me in the line had given four swabs. Four. I saw him. He walked out holding the little cards they gave you like a hand of poker that had lost.
They told me about my mother on the eighteenth of August. They’d found her days before. It took that long for the swab to match.

They found her on top of the seawall on Front Street. Sitting, the man from the county said, very gently, standing in the doorway of the hotel room. Sitting up. Facing the sea. He didn’t say anything else about it and I didn’t ask. Later I learned that a lot of the people who died were found in their cars on Front Street, in the jam, trying to get out, and some in their houses, and some near the water. Most of them were old. That’s the thing nobody says enough. Most of the people who died in Lahaina were old, older than sixty, the people who couldn’t run, who couldn’t climb walls, who’d never in their lives gone past their knees.
My mother was sitting on the wall above the place where a stranger had held her grandson in the water all night.
She’d stayed. She’d stayed on the wall. Right there. Above him. I knew why. I didn’t know yet how I knew. I just knew.

She couldn’t swim. She couldn’t climb down. She couldn’t see him in the dark, not once, not all night. So she did the one thing that was left to a woman with bad ankles and a voice that could reach the end of the lane. She sat where he could find her. Like a porch light you leave on. Like that plastic chair on the lanai every afternoon, when he came up the lane from the harbor dripping and late, and she shouted at him, and he knew from the shouting that he was home. She kept her place. That’s all. She kept her place all night, so that if he looked up, there would be somebody there.

When the man from the county left I closed the door and sat down on the hotel carpet with my back against the door and put my face into my knees, and I made a sound I’d never made before, a sound that came up from somewhere under my stomach, and I couldn’t stop it. My son was asleep on the bed. He didn’t wake up. Or he woke up and didn’t move. I’ll never know which.
The hotel. I should tell you about the hotel.

After the fire there were thousands of us with nowhere to live. Eight, ten thousand people, they said, whose homes were gone. And the island had hotels. Big, beautiful, empty hotels, because the tourists had all left. So the Red Cross and the government paid the hotels to take us in. That was the plan, and it was a good plan, I’m not saying it wasn’t. We got a room. Clean sheets. A shower. A view of the ocean.
They put us in a resort in Kāʻanapali.

They put us in my resort. The one where I worked. Same building. Same tower. Same long hallways with the same patterned carpet I’d vacuumed ten thousand times. We were on the fourth floor. A garden-view king. I knew that room. I’d cleaned that room. I knew which drawer stuck and which light switch was backward.
And two weeks after the fire, they called me back to work. Same job. The resort needed housekeepers, and I needed money, and the rooms were full of families like mine, and somebody had to clean them.

So that’s what I did. For months. In the morning I got up in a hotel room, and dressed my silent son, and took him to the room downstairs where volunteers watched the kids, and then I went to the laundry and got my cart, my own cart, with my name still taped on the handle, and I went up the stairs and cleaned the rooms of people who’d lost their homes in the same fire as me, and they left me five dollars on the pillow, some of them, which was one of the worst things that happened to me that year, and I took it.
Keola didn’t speak.

Not in the hotel. Not in the playroom with the volunteers. Not to me. He’d nod. He’d shake his head. He’d eat a little, if I put food in front of him and sat there. He’d let me hold him. At night he’d sleep pressed against my back so hard I could feel the bones of his face against my spine. But no words came out of him, not one, not for weeks, and then not for months. The only word he’d said since the fire was the one he said to that man in the gym: Uncle. A doctor came, a woman who works with children after terrible things. She sat on the floor with him and some crayons. She told me afterward that it happens, that children sometimes go quiet when what’s inside them is too big to say, that it’s a way of holding very still till the danger passes. That he’d speak when he was ready. That I shouldn’t push.

I didn’t push. I’m not much of a pusher. I just waited, and cleaned rooms, and every night I lay in that bed I used to make and listened to him breathing, and I thought about the haole man in the gym, his face when he understood. Where’s mine?
I thought about his boy, whose name I knew. Theo. Theo, Theo, you’re okay, bud.

I found out later that the name was on the list, near the end, under T. Talbert, Theo, 9, visitor, Ohio. For weeks it was there. Then they took the list down. They said there were only a few names left, and they’d keep looking. Then there were fewer. Then the names that were left, they stopped saying out loud.
They never found him. I’ll say that now, plainly, so you don’t wait for it. The sea didn’t give him back.
20. The Weight Wes
I stayed on Maui three weeks.
I don’t know how to tell you about those weeks, so here is what I did.

I gave them my cheek. They swabbed it, both sides, so they could match me against whatever they found. I stood at the edge of the burn zone every day, at the fence they’d put up, at the line of police tape, and I watched the men in white suits and masks go in with their dogs. The dogs were trained to find people. That’s all I’ll say about the dogs. I talked to the Coast Guard. A lieutenant with a kind, square face sat with me on a bench at the harbor up the coast and told me, without hurrying, what the currents do along that coast. How the wind that night was blowing straight out to sea. How anything in the water near the wall would have been carried out, through the gaps in the reef, into the channel. How the channel there is very deep. He used that word. Deep. He said they’d searched. He said they’d keep looking. He said he was sorry, and he meant it, I could tell. He’d said it before. He’d say it again that week. He was still saying it with care. I liked him for that.

I went to the hotel where they were putting up the visitors who’d lost everything, and I slept there, or didn’t sleep. They gave me a room with a view of the channel. I sat on the lanai at night and looked at the black water and the lights of Lānaʻi across it and I thought: he’s out there. Somewhere out there, between here and there. In the deep part.
Will she be scared? In the deep part?
I found out about Claire on the ninth day.

That’s how I think about it, even now: I found out about Claire. As if she were a fact I’d learned, like the depth of the channel. I was in the hotel room, going through what I had left, which was nothing: the borrowed T-shirt, the donated shorts, and the backpack. The firefighters had peeled it off me on the street that night and somebody had put it in a plastic bag with my name on it, and the bag had followed me to the hospital and back, and I hadn’t looked at it. That day I took it out and looked.

The long gash down the side. The strap half torn off. Empty. Wallet, phone, water, inhaler, gone. And the inside of the bag, all the inside of the bag, every seam and corner, the bottom, the zipper teeth, was coated with a fine pale gray powder. Dried now. Not ash. I knew ash by then, I’d had it in my hair and teeth for a week. This was different. Finer. Paler. Grittier. Like the finest sand.

I sat on the floor of that hotel room with the bag in my lap and rubbed a little of it between my fingers, and I remembered the water that night. The pale cloud that came and went around us with the waves. The haze in the water. The flour-fine dust on my arms and on the boy’s chest when I looked down. Ash, I’d thought. That’s the town.

She’d gone in. The bag had torn in the rocks, in the blast, and the inner bag with it, and she’d gone into the water. All five pounds of her. Not from a boat. Not in the channel where we’d seen the whales. Not on a calm blue morning with Theo holding my hand and the two of us saying something we’d written down beforehand. At the bottom of a seawall in a burning town, in the dark, in the smoke, while I held a stranger’s child.
The same night as him. The same water.

I sat there a long time with the gray on my fingertips. I didn’t wipe it off. I want to be careful how I say this, because it isn’t a pretty thing and I won’t make it one. It was the last of her that wasn’t in the sea: a little dust in the seams of a torn bag. They had gone into the water together, the two of them, within the same minute, and I had been there, an arm’s length away, and I hadn’t known. I had put my hand in her and called it ash. I had watched her slide off my fingers and thought, that’s the town. The afternoon light went across the carpet while I sat there, and up the far side of the room, and off it, and I didn’t get up to turn on the lamp.
I’d promised her somewhere warm.

I don’t want to tell you about the flight home, so I won’t. I’ll tell you only that I flew back alone, and that the airline, when I told them at the check-in desk why there was only one of us, gave me a seat with nobody next to me, and that I sat in that row and looked out the window as the plane came up over the channel, and I saw the water from above again. The palest green near the shore, then the bright turquoise, then the bruise-dark patches of the reef, and then, all at once, as if somebody had drawn it with a ruler, the deep.
The deep blue. The blue that went down.
I put my hand flat on the window, like a kid.

I didn’t say anything. There was nobody to say it to. But in my head, very clearly, in my own voice, I heard myself say, Theo, look. Just that. Theo, look. And then the plane turned, and the island went under the wing, and was gone.
21. We Buy Lahaina Kanoe
The texts started coming before the fire was fully out.
Not just to me. To everybody. I’d be in the hotel room, or in the laundry, or at the shelter picking up diapers for my cousin’s baby, and my phone would buzz, and it would be a number I didn’t know.
Aloha, so sorry for your loss. We are local investors interested in purchasing your Lahaina property, any condition, cash, fast close. Call anytime.
Aloha [ah-LOH-hah] is our hello and our goodbye and our love, all in one word. They used it to sell.
Hi! Saw your property on Lahainaluna. We buy as-is. No repairs needed.
As-is. My house was ash. As-is.
Lahaina Strong! Let us take the stress away. We pay cash for land.

I’d never told anybody my phone number except family and work and the dentist. They had it anyway. Everybody’s. You could find anyone’s name and address and phone number from the county property records in about five minutes, somebody explained to me later, if you knew how and had the motivation. Somebody had the motivation. Somebody was sitting somewhere going down a list of burned addresses, address by address, with a cup of coffee, texting widows.

I didn’t answer. Nobody I knew answered. Bully wrote back to one of them, from the next room in the hotel, a long text with a lot of words in it I won’t repeat. He showed it to me afterward. It was very creative.

The Governor went on TV a week or so after the fire and said he was going to try to stop it. He said he’d look for a way to put a pause on land sales in Lahaina, so that families wouldn’t be pressured to sell to outsiders while they were still grieving. He said, more or less, Lahaina will remain in Hawaiian hands. I watched it on the hotel TV, sitting on the edge of the bed I used to make. I wanted to believe him. I think he meant it. I don’t think he could do it. You can’t stop people selling their own land if they want to, it turns out. Not for long. Not legally. And a lot of people would want to. A lot of people had a mortgage on a house that was gone, and no job, and the rent somewhere else on the island was already more than they’d ever paid. A lot of people would get tired. That’s what the texts were waiting for. They weren’t in a hurry. They had all the time in the world. They just needed you to get tired.
In October they reopened West Maui to tourists.

The Governor said it had to happen. He said it on TV again, and he wasn’t wrong, exactly. Tourism is the island’s work. It’s most of the jobs. Everybody I knew, my cousins, the boys from the activity desk, Bully’s nephew who drove a tour van, all of them needed the tourists back, needed the paycheck, needed the five dollars on the pillow. So the hotels started taking visitors again, a little at a time, starting at the far north end and working down.

And so there were mornings, that autumn, when I would walk out of the hotel lobby with my son to take him to the school they’d set up for the Lahaina kids in a borrowed building, and in the lobby there’d be a family just arriving, with suitcases and sunburn and leis [LAYZ], necklaces of flowers, round their necks, sweet and fresh, being welcomed by the front desk girl, who was my second cousin, and whose house was also gone. And the family would step aside to let us by, politely. And they would not know. There was no reason they’d know. We looked like anybody.

Some of us went to the beach. You might have seen that too. People from Lahaina set up chairs and coolers and fishing poles on the beach in front of the big Kāʻanapali hotels, right on the sand, and stayed there. Every day. For months. They called it a fish-in. They were fishing, sort of, but they were really sitting. Sitting where the tourists could see them, holding signs, saying in the most polite way possible: we’re still here. We’re your housekeepers and your cooks and your bus drivers and we’re living in your hotel and we have nowhere to go. They wanted the government to do something about the vacation rentals, the thousands of apartments and houses on the island that were rented to tourists by the week instead of to families by the year, because if those went back to families, there’d be somewhere for us to live.

There’s a word we have, kuleana [koo-leh-AH-nah]. It means responsibility, but it also means the right that comes with it, both at once, like two sides of one coin. If the land feeds you, you have the kuleana to care for it, and you also have the right to stay on it. That’s what the people on the beach were saying, really. Not give us something. Just: this is our kuleana. We’re not going anywhere.

I went once. I sat on a cooler next to an old man with a fishing pole with no hook on it, and we looked out at the water together, and a woman in a big hat walked past us with her husband and said, not unkindly, “Oh, look, honey, the locals are fishing,” and he said, “Isn’t that nice.”

They let us go back to see the houses in October. Not to stay. To look. You had to make an appointment and go in a group, and they gave you a white suit made of paper, with a hood, and gloves and booties and a mask, because the ash was full of poisons. Old paint, old pipes, the chemicals they’d put on the cane a hundred years ago, the batteries from all the cars. All of it burned together and lying there in a gray powder a foot deep.
I took Keola. I don’t know if that was right. The doctor said I could, if he wanted. I asked him if he wanted to and he nodded.

We walked up the lane in our white suits, holding hands. It was like walking on the moon. Everything gray. Everything flat. You could see straight through to the mountain from the sea, because there was nothing left standing in between. Just the black trunks of trees, here and there, and the chimneys of a few houses that had them, and car frames, rusted orange already, and twisted metal, and the gray.

The lane wasn’t a lane. It was a gray place with shapes in it. I found our house by the concrete steps. Three steps going up to nothing. And the slab the house had stood on, covered in ash and broken glass and black curls of melted tin from the roof.

In the corner where the kitchen had been there was the rice cooker. Black. Melted on one side. Its lid fused shut. It was sitting there on the slab where the counter used to be, upright, like it was waiting for someone to push the button.
I’d left my note under it. The morning of the fire. No power. Went work. Charge phone in car if you need. Love you.

I stood there looking at that rice cooker and something broke in me that I won’t describe, and I let it break, and I stood there in my white paper suit in the middle of what used to be my house and cried until the mask was wet through. Keola stood next to me and held my gloved hand and didn’t say anything. He was looking at something.
He was looking at the gate. Where the gate had been.

The angel’s trumpet tree was dead. Burned down to a black stump, just a jagged stick of charcoal knee-high. But at the base of it, out of the black, out of the gray, there was something green. Three leaves. Big, soft, new, pale green, the size of my hand. Pushing up out of the burned root.

Keola let go of my hand and went over and crouched down in front of it, in his little white suit, the paper rustling, and he looked at those three leaves for a long time. And he didn’t touch them. He knew better. Every bit of it is poison. Tūtū told him that the first day he could walk to the gate.
