I watched him from the slab. A little white paper boy crouched in a gray world, not touching. He put his gloved hands on his knees to keep them still. He looked at those leaves the way he’d looked up at that tree when he was three, mouth shut tight, for a long time, like they might reach down and get him. And I thought: she’s still teaching him. Even now. Even burned down to a stick. Here is a pretty thing. Here is what it can do. Don’t touch. Remember.
Somebody has to remember what pretty things can do.
22. Three in the Morning Wes

The pool at my school in Ohio is lit from under the water. You come in at five-thirty on a winter morning before practice, when it’s still black outside and snowing, and you don’t turn on the overhead lights yet, and the water is glowing, a clear blue light coming up out of it, throwing wobbling ripples of light onto the ceiling. I used to love that. I used to stand in the doorway with my coffee for a minute, before the kids came, and watch the light move on the ceiling, and feel lucky to have a job where that was the first thing I saw every day.

I went back to work in October. The school was very kind. Everybody was very kind. My kids, my swimmers, sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds, made a banner and hung it on the wall of the pool, a long white bedsheet with blue letters: WE LOVE YOU COACH. Underneath it somebody had painted a little blue wave. They’d all signed it. I stood in front of it on my first morning back and couldn’t move.
I could coach. I could stand on the deck and blow the whistle and call out times and tell a girl to tuck her chin on the turn. I was good at it. I was still good at it.
I couldn’t get in.

Every time I stood at the edge, at the deep end, and looked down at the water, at the black line on the bottom twelve feet down, wobbling in the light, I felt it in the backs of my knees, the way you feel a high place. I can’t see what’s under it. And I’d step back, and go and stand somewhere else.
At night I read.

I don’t sleep much now. I wake up at three, most nights, the same time every night, as if something is setting an alarm in me. I used to lie there. Now I get up and go downstairs and sit at the kitchen table with my laptop, in the dark, with the snow falling outside the window over the back porch where Claire used to stand in thunderstorms, and I read about the fire. Everything. Every report, every timeline, every article, every interview with every survivor. Over that winter and the year after, I read the official investigations as they came out, what the fire scientists said and what the government’s investigators said. I’ve read what the power company said and what the lawyers suing the power company said.
And I’ve read the other things. The things people put on the internet at three in the morning.

You know some of them. Everybody does. That the fire was set on purpose. That it was started from space, by a laser, a secret weapon, and they’ll show you pictures of a beam of light coming down from the sky that is, if you look at it for a second with a clear head, a picture of something else entirely, an old photo from a rocket launch or a transformer blowing up somewhere far away. That everything blue survived, blue cars, blue roofs, blue umbrellas, because the laser couldn’t burn blue. That it was all a plan to clear the land and build some kind of computer-run city. That the death toll was really thousands and they were hiding the bodies, all the children, especially the children.

I’ve looked and looked, and there’s nothing in those. The pictures are other pictures. The blue things didn’t survive because they were blue; plenty of blue things burned, and the things that didn’t burn, didn’t burn for ordinary reasons, a metal roof, a gap between the house and the next one, a wind that turned. The death toll, by the end, was a hundred and two, every one of them counted by name. The few who were never found, like my son, were kept on a separate list. I know because I watched them keep him on it.

But I understand why people believe it. Because at three in the morning, a laser from space is easier. A laser from space means somebody did it on purpose, somebody evil, somebody you can hate with your whole heart. It means it was a plan. A plan is better than what really happened. What really happened is that nobody planned anything. A power line came down in the wind onto dry grass, and the grass was there because the sugar left and nobody cut it, and the hydrants ran dry, and the sirens didn’t sound, and the phones didn’t work, and the fire that was out wasn’t out, and a hundred small things went wrong one after another, each one ordinary, each one somebody’s ordinary mistake on an ordinary bad day, and they all added up, and my son is at the bottom of the channel.
There’s no one to hate for that. That’s what’s unbearable. You can’t hate a hundred small things.
So some people make one big thing out of them, so they’ll have someone to hate. I understand that.

I don’t do it. I’d like to say it’s because I’m too smart. It isn’t. It’s because I’m a coach, and I know what it’s like when a kid drowns in a pool. I’ve never had it happen. Thank God. But I’ve been to the trainings, a dozen of them, and they all say the same thing: it’s never one thing. It’s never a monster. It’s the lifeguard looking away for nine seconds to answer a question, and the pool being a little too crowded, and the kid’s friend saying come on, it’s not that deep. It’s always a hundred small things.
I know about a hundred small things. I held the wrong boy.
Some of what people said, I couldn’t dismiss. Here it is, in a row.

That the power company didn’t switch off the lines. That’s true. The company that runs the electricity on Maui didn’t have a plan for shutting off power ahead of a dangerous wind, the way the big power companies in California do now. They knew the wind was coming. The weather people had said so for days. They left the lines on. The lines came down on the grass. The lawyers say that’s why. The company says its lines had been switched off for hours by the time the afternoon fire started, and that the afternoon fire was the morning fire coming back to life, which is what the investigators finally said too. Both of those things can be true. The morning fire was theirs. And the afternoon fire was the morning fire.

That the power company had talked for years about making its lines safer against fire, about stronger poles and covered wires and cutting back the brush, and that most of that work hadn’t been done. That’s true too. You can read about it.
That the water was held up. That a man asked for stream water for the reservoirs on the day of the fire and was told to wait. That’s true. Whether it would have mattered, nobody knows.
That the sirens were silent. True. That the man who could have sounded them said he was afraid people would run toward the fire. True. That he quit nine days later. True.
That somebody started texting people offering to buy their burned land within days. True. I’ve seen the texts. A woman I know sent me pictures of them.

None of that’s a laser. None of it’s a plan. All of it’s real. You can put it in a row and look at it and decide for yourself what kind of thing it is. Whether it’s a hundred small things, or something more.
I don’t know. I’ve looked at it every night for months.

The woman I know is Kanoe. I should tell you that. She sent me a letter in November. The first one. Handwritten, on hotel notepaper, with the hotel’s name at the top. She’ll tell you about it herself.
I’m still sitting here. It’s three in the morning. It’s snowing.
23. What Tūtū Did Kanoe
Keola spoke on the twenty-fourth of November. The day after Thanksgiving.

We’d had Thanksgiving in a ballroom. The hotel had put on a big dinner for all the fire families living there, turkey and stuffing and kālua [KAH-loo-ah] pig, which is pork cooked slow in an underground oven, and rice, and mac salad, which is macaroni in mayonnaise, and poi. Hundreds of us, at long tables with white cloths, under chandeliers. Some people sang. Some people cried. Everybody ate too much because nobody knew what else to do with their hands. Keola ate two plates and fell asleep with his head on the table, and Bully carried him upstairs.

The next morning I woke up early. It was still dark. I was lying on my side facing the window with Keola against my back, the way he always slept, his face pressed to my spine. And I felt him wake up. I felt his breathing change.
And then he said, into my back, very quietly, in a voice that cracked from not being used:
“Mama. Tūtū gave me to Uncle.”

His voice was different. Lower, rough, with the whistle still in it where his teeth were gone. Three months I’d waited for it. I’d lain in that bed every night listening to him breathe and trying to remember exactly how he sounded, and I was starting to lose it, the way you lose a song you haven’t heard in a long time. And here it was, against my spine, in the dark. I felt the words before I heard them. They came through his chest into my back.

I didn’t move. I didn’t turn around. I was afraid if I turned around he’d stop. I held still the way you hold still when a bird lands near you. I lay there with my heart going and the dark window in front of me and I said, as gently as I could, “Tell me, baby.”
And he told me.

He told me how the fire came down the lane. How Tūtū was in the kitchen and he was in the yard with his ball and the smoke came over the roof all at once, black, and there was fire in Uncle Bully’s mango tree three houses down, and Tūtū came out on the lanai and looked, just for a second, and said, “Keola. Shoes. Now.” And he didn’t even get his shoes. He went in his bare feet. How she took his hand and they went out the gate, past the angel’s trumpet, and she said, “Makai. We go makai. To the water. The water always goes home and so do we.”

He told me how they walked down the hill toward the sea. How she couldn’t go fast. How the fire was in the trees on both sides and the wind was full of burning leaves and Tūtū kept her free hand over his head the whole way down, like an umbrella, and burning leaves landed on her arm and she just brushed them off and kept walking. How there were cars in the street not moving, people screaming, and a man on the corner of Front Street with a garden hose spraying it in the air like it would help.

He told me about the wall. The haole Uncle with the boy around his neck. The boy who was screaming I can’t, I can’t. He said, “It was the scared boy, Mama. From the harbor. The one who wouldn’t swim. I told him the water was nice.”
He told me what Tūtū said. He told me exactly. He was eight and he’d been carrying it in his mouth for three months, shut tight, so he had it exactly.
You hold him. You don’t let go. Whatever.
Go with Uncle. I’ll be right here. I’ll be right here on the wall.
Take my life.

I lay there with my eyes open in the dark and the tears running sideways off my nose onto the pillow, and I understood what my mother had said. What she’d meant. Not my life is over. Not save yourself. She’d handed my son to a stranger and told him the boy’s name in words the stranger couldn’t know were a name.
Keola. The life. She’d said, take my life. She’d said, take Keola.
She’d said my life. The way she always did. Good night, my life.

He told me the rest. How they went in the water. How it hit them. How he held Uncle’s backpack strap, and how the other boy, the scared boy, was holding Uncle’s neck and crying, and how Uncle kept counting, out loud, one, two, three, here it comes, hold, and how Uncle had a nice voice for counting.
He told me about the bang.

“It was so loud, Mama. It was like the whole world. And the wave came and I went under and I let go of the backpack and I was rolling and rolling and then I came up and I couldn’t see nothing. Smoke. And I heard Uncle yelling. Theo! Theo! So I swam to Uncle. Because he was yelling. And I bumped into him and he grabbed me.”
“And he thought you were Theo.”

“Yeah.” A long silence. His breath on my back. “He said I got you, bud. He was crying. He was holding me so tight. And I knew I wasn’t Theo, Mama. I knew. But he was crying and I didn’t want him to stop holding me.”
“Oh, baby.”
“So I didn’t say.”
I waited. I could feel there was more. I could feel it in his breathing, the way he was holding still, the way you hold still on top of a wave before it breaks.
“Mama.”
“Yes, baby.”
“After the bang. When I came up. When I was swimming to Uncle.” His voice went very small. “I heard the other boy.”
I didn’t say anything. I couldn’t.
“He was yelling Dad. Dad, Dad. By the rocks. In the smoke. I couldn’t see him. I heard him.” A long silence. “Then the wave came again. And I didn’t hear him.”

He was crying now. Finally, after three months, he was crying, against my back, big ugly sobs that shook the whole bed, and I turned over at last and held him against my chest, my son, my life, and he said into me, over and over, “I didn’t say, Mama, I didn’t tell Uncle, I didn’t say,” and I said, “It’s not yours, baby, it’s not yours, it’s not your fault, you were eight, you were in the water, it’s not yours,” and I held him until the window went gray and then gold and the sun came up over the black mountain.

After he slept I got up and took the hotel notepad from the desk, with the hotel’s name across the top in gold, and the hotel pen, and I sat on the floor by the window and I wrote a letter to the haole man.

I knew his name by then. Talbert. Everybody in the shelters knew it. The man from Ohio who lost his son at the seawall. I got his address from a woman at the family center who probably shouldn’t have given it to me.

I wrote down everything Keola told me. All of it. I didn’t make it nicer. I thought he’d want to know. I thought, if it were me, I’d want to know every single thing, even the worst thing, especially the worst thing, because the worst thing I can imagine is always worse than the worst thing that happened.
I told him what my mother said on the wall. I told him what it meant. I told him my son’s name.

At the end I wrote: I’m sorry. I’m sorry about Theo. Keola says he was a nice boy. Keola says he wanted to see the deep part, for his mother. He whispered it to Keola in the water, before the bang, between the waves, while you were counting. I’m sorry about your wife too. Keola says the scared boy told him his mom was in your bag.
My mother stayed on the wall all night above you. They found her there. I think she was singing. I think you heard her. I think she was singing to both boys.
You held my son. I don’t know what to say about that. I’m grateful. I’m so angry. I’m sorry. I don’t know which one is true. All of them, I think.
Thank you. — Kanoe
I put it in an envelope from the front desk and gave it to my second cousin, who was working the desk that morning, and she put a stamp on it and didn’t ask me anything.
Said in the Harbor

Let me tell you what they’ll do now, up there. I know because I’ve seen it before. Not here, maybe. Not this town. But it always goes the same way, everywhere, every time a town burns or floods or falls into me. It goes like a tide. You can set your watch by it.
First they’ll ask who did it.

That’s right. That’s what they should ask. And some of the answers will be plain and some will be crooked, and they’ll come out slowly, over months, over years, in reports with long names. They’ll say the power lines did it. A line came down in the wind onto the grass in the morning, they’ll say, and sparked, and they’ll say the fire that came back in the afternoon was the same fire, not out, only sleeping. They’ll find that the company that ran the lines had no plan to turn them off in a bad wind, though other companies in other places did. They’ll find that the company had talked for years about making its lines safer against fire, and that most of the work was still waiting. They’ll find the company had paid its owners their share every year while the safety work waited. Some will say these are the same fact. Some will say they aren’t.

They’ll find that the grass was there because the sugar left and nobody tended the land after, and that people had warned about that grass for years, at meeting after meeting, and the grass grew back taller after every meeting.

They’ll find that the sirens were silent, and that the man in charge of them said he feared they’d send people running uphill, into the fire. Some will believe him. Some will say a siren is a siren, and a frightened person can be told which way to run.

They’ll find the hydrants went soft. They’ll find the pipes melted in the houses and I ran out through the broken ends onto the ground. They’ll find that on the day of the fire, a request to put more of me into the reservoirs waited for hours on a desk. They’ll argue for years about whether that mattered. Some will say it couldn’t have. Some will say: then why did you make him wait?

They’ll find that some roads were blocked, by fallen poles and live wires, and by crews and officers turning cars back from those wires, and that people sat in their cars on Front Street with the fire coming because there was nowhere to turn. Some will say: they were keeping people from being electrocuted. Some will say: they kept us in. Both of them were there. Both of them saw what they saw.
Then they’ll ask who pays.

And that will take a long time, and it will be lawyers, and it will be numbers so large they stop sounding like money. In the end, the power company and the landowners and the county and the state and others will agree together to pay something over four billion dollars to the people who lost everything, and none of them will admit that they did anything wrong, which is how such agreements are written. Then the insurance companies will go to court and argue about who gets to take what out of it, because they paid too, for the houses, and they’ll want their money back. Ordinary people will wait in hotel rooms while this happens.
Then they’ll ask who gets the land.

They’ll text the widows. They’ll call the old men. Cash. Fast. As-is. The Governor will say no one should be pressured to sell, and he’ll mean it, and it will help a little and not enough. Somebody will remember that the land under that town was taken once already, a hundred and fifty years ago, piece by piece, by the sugar men, and the water with it. Somebody will look at the burned lots by the sea, the best land on the island, with its view of the channel, cleared now, flat, ready, and they will say out loud the thing a lot of people are thinking. Isn’t this convenient. Isn’t it convenient for somebody.
That’s the strongest of the stories they’ll tell. I want you to look at it closely.

Here’s what’s real in it: the lots will be worth a great deal. People with money will want them. Some families will sell, because they’re tired, because the rent somewhere else is more than they ever paid, because the insurance won’t cover what it costs to rebuild now. In the years after, the island will have to fight hard, in law after law, to keep the town for the people who were born in it. And the fight will be real, and not all of it will be won.
Here’s what isn’t in it, as far as anyone has found: a hand that lit the match. A meeting where somebody said burn it. No one has ever found that. Many have looked.

So you’ll have to decide, the way every person on this island will have to decide. Was it a plan? Or was it something worse than a plan? A plan, at least, is somebody’s. Something worse is no one’s. A hundred small hungers, each of them ordinary, each one sure it had a good reason, all of them leaning the same way, downhill, like water. That’s what I’d tell you, if you asked me. But you’re right not to take my word. I’m not neutral. I was taken too.

And then there’ll be the other stories. You’ll hear them. The ones about lights from the sky and secret weapons, about blue things that couldn’t burn, about cities run by machines, about thousands of hidden dead. I’ll say this about them once and then leave them in the dark where they belong: they aren’t true, and the people who need them most aren’t stupid. They’re grieving. They’d rather have a monster than a hundred small things. A monster you can fight.
I’m not a monster. Neither was the fire. Neither was the wind. We only did what we do. It’s people who choose. Who gets the water. Who gets the land. Who gets told to wait, and who doesn’t.
The tide goes out. The tide comes in. The questions will go on longer than any of the people asking them.
I’ll be here for the answer, whenever it comes. I have nowhere else to be.
V. THE FLOAT
24. One Year Wes
I came back on the sixth of August, a year later, almost to the day.

I came in on the same approach. I’d asked for a window seat on the left side. The woman at the desk in Ohio didn’t ask why. The plane came down out of the high white clouds over the channel, and there it was, the water, all its colors laid out below me like a map somebody had painted by hand. Pale green, bright turquoise, the dark bruises of the reef, and the ruled line where the bottom falls away and the blue goes down.

I didn’t put my hand on the window this time. I’d decided I wouldn’t. I just looked. I looked at the deep part for as long as the plane let me, the whole long slow turn in over the island, and I thought about a lieutenant with a square kind face on a bench at a harbor, saying deep, and meaning it carefully.

I didn’t stay in Lahaina. You couldn’t. Most of it was still behind fences. I stayed up the coast in a small, cheap hotel with a view of a parking lot, and on the seventh I drove down and parked as close as I could get and walked along the fences.
I’m going to tell you what it looked like a year later, since I’ve told you what it looked like before, and during.

It was clean. That’s what struck me first. A year of work by thousands of people in white suits and hard hats, with trucks and machines, had taken away the ash and the rubble and the burned cars. The town wasn’t gray anymore. It was brown. Lot after lot of bare, scraped, packed brown dirt, each one marked off at its corners with little stakes and orange ribbon, each one with a concrete slab or a set of steps or just nothing, and between them the streets, swept, empty, with grass already pushing up in the cracks. Here and there a stone wall. A single chimney. The black trunk of a tree with no branches, standing like a post. On some of the lots people had put up things: a cross made of two burned beams, a painted sign that said WE WILL RETURN, a ring of white stones with a plastic lei on it, a child’s bicycle painted all over in bright flowers. On one lot somebody had planted a single banana tree, already taller than me, its big leaves shining.

You could see from the mountain to the sea. Nothing was in the way. From the fence at the top of the town you could look straight down Lahainaluna Road, a mile of brown dirt and stakes and ribbon, all the way to the blue water at the bottom, and Lānaʻi floating there across the channel exactly as it had floated for a million years. It was the most beautiful view in the world. It had been, all along, hidden behind a town.
The banyan was alive.

I’d heard. Everybody had heard. It had been in the news all year, the tree that survived. But I hadn’t believed it until I stood in front of it. It was fenced, and propped, and there were hoses running in among the roots, and somebody had built little shade screens around some of the trunks. Half of it was still black, the bark scorched, the hanging roots burned off short. But all through the top of it, all over the old gray arms, there were leaves. Green leaves. Not many, not the great roaring crown I’d stood under with my son in the wind. Patches. Tufts. Bright, new, shining, the green of the inside of a cucumber, coming out of black wood.
I stood at the fence. An old man was standing there too, a local man, with a cane and a straw hat. He didn’t look at me. He said, after a while, to the tree, “Still here.”
“Yeah,” I said.
“They said it was going to die.” He nodded at it. “Tree don’t listen.”
I walked down to the seawall last.

Most of Front Street was still fenced. But for the anniversary they’d opened a stretch of the seawall where people could come, with a gap in the fence and a volunteer at a folding table. I found the stretch. I knew it. I don’t know how. Everything was different, the buildings across the road gone, just brown lots and orange ribbon where the T-shirt shop had been. But the wall was the same wall. The same concrete, waist-high, with the flat top. The same black rocks below it. The same water coming in on the rocks, green and gold in the afternoon light, slapping and sucking, gentle, ordinary, as if nothing had ever happened here.

People had left things on the wall. All along it. Flowers, dried and fresh. Leis, dozens of them, hung over the edge. Stones with names painted on them. Candles in jars, burned out. Photos in plastic sleeves, faded by a year of sun. A pair of rubber slippers, men’s slippers, side by side, very neat, with a white flower in each one.
I stood in front of those slippers for a long time.

Then I took out of my pocket the thing I’d brought. It was a pair of swim goggles. Kid’s goggles, blue, with a strap that had been knotted to make it shorter. Theo’s. The pair he’d never once put on over his eyes at the Y, the pair I’d packed for Hawaii in case. He’d left them on the back seat of the rental car after the beach on Friday. The apartment was gone. But the rental car had been in the lot six blocks north, and the lot hadn’t burned. Of all the things. Of all the things in that whole town, a parking lot. The rental company found the goggles on the back seat and mailed them to Ohio in October, in a padded envelope, with a note saying they were sorry for my loss and had waived all fees.

I put the goggles on the wall, next to the slippers. I sat down on the wall with my legs over the sea, where the old woman had sat. And I didn’t say anything to anybody, because there was nobody to say it to, and I looked at the water.
25. Take My Life Kanoe

We’d been writing letters all year. Not many. Five or six, each way. His were typed and short and very careful, like he was afraid of using too many words. Mine were on whatever paper I had. When the hotel moved us out in the spring, into an apartment an hour away on the other side of the island, three rooms, nothing on the walls, rented through some program the state set up, I wrote him on the back of the moving forms.
He wrote me in July that he was coming back for the anniversary. He asked if he could see Keola. He said he’d understand if not.

I asked Keola. He was nine by then. He’d grown two inches and his new front teeth had come in, big and crooked. He talked now. Not like before. He’d never be the boy who screamed off the harbor wall again. But he talked. He thought about it for a whole day, and then at dinner he said, “Yeah. I want to see Uncle.”

We met at the beach just south of town where the water’s calm behind the reef. His idea. He said it was where he’d tried to teach his son to swim. He said he didn’t know if that was a good reason or a bad one.

I saw him before he saw us. He was sitting on the sand above the waterline with his knees pulled up, the way a kid sits, looking at the water. Thinner than in the gym. Gray at the sides of his head, more than a year’s worth. A sunburn already on the back of his neck. He had the look of a man who’s carried something heavy for a long way and put it down and doesn’t know what to do with his arms.
Keola let go of my hand and walked down the beach toward him, ahead of me. Not running. Walking. He stopped in front of him.
“Hi, Uncle.”
The man looked up. I saw his face do what I knew it would. I saw him see my son, alive, nine, brown, standing in the sun with his new crooked teeth. I saw him see the other boy who wasn’t there.
“Hi,” he said. “Hi, Keola.”
He knew the name now. I’d told him in my first letter. He said it carefully, every sound in its place, the way you’d pick up something that might break.

We sat on the sand, the three of us, in a row, and watched the water for a while. A sea turtle came in, a big one, and put its old face up and breathed out, pff, like a tired man sitting down, and went on.
“That’s the same turtle,” Wes said.
“How you know?” said Keola.
“I don’t. It just feels like it.”
“Could be,” Keola said seriously. “They live like a hundred years.”
When Keola went down to the water’s edge to look for shells, Wes and I talked.
I’m not going to tell you all of it. Some of it was ours. I’ll tell you this.

He told me he had read every word I’d written him a hundred times. He told me he still woke up at three in the morning. He told me he coached his swimmers and couldn’t get in the pool. He told me his wife had gone into the water that night, from the torn bag, at the bottom of the wall. The same night. The same water as his son. He said it very plainly, looking at the sea. He said, “So she got her wish. She’s somewhere warm.”

I told him about my mother. About the bank, and the pencil in her hair, and the plastic chair on the lanai, and how she hollered at Bully about the news for forty years. I told him she’d never been past her knees in the ocean in her whole life. Seventy-nine years on an island and she never went past her knees.
“She told me that,” he said. “On the wall.”
“She said something else to you,” I said. “On the wall. Keola told me. I wrote it to you.”
“Take my life.”
“You know what it means now.”
“I know what it means.” He was quiet for a long time. Then he said the thing I think he’d come all the way from Ohio to say.

“I didn’t take it. That’s the thing. She gave him to me, and told me to hold him, whatever, and I didn’t. I lost him. In the dark. I lost both of them. And then I grabbed the first one that came. I didn’t take her life. I took whatever bumped into me. If it had been Theo who bumped into me, I’d have held Theo all night, and told myself your boy was fine because he could swim, and he’d have been fine, maybe, he swam to me, didn’t he, he’d have swum to somebody. Or he wouldn’t. I don’t know. I don’t know. I didn’t choose. That’s what I can’t stand. I didn’t save your son. I just didn’t let go of him.”
The water came in and went out.
“Wes,” I said. I’d never said his name out loud before. “That’s what she asked you to do.”
He looked at me.

“She didn’t say save him. She didn’t say choose. She was seventy-nine years old and smart as anything, she knew nobody can promise to save anybody in a fire. She said hold him. Don’t let go. Whatever.” I put my hand flat on the sand between us. “You didn’t let go. All night. With smoke in your head. With your own boy gone. You held on to a stranger’s kid and you didn’t let go. That’s what she asked. You did it.”
“I did it to the wrong boy.”

“There was no wrong boy.” I didn’t know I was going to say it until I said it, and it came out harder than I meant, and I didn’t take it back. “There was two boys and one man and the whole sea. There was no wrong boy. There was two boys and you couldn’t hold them both, and nobody could, and you know that, you know it better than me, you’re a coach, you know what a person can hold in the water. You held one. That’s what a person can do. Don’t you dare call my son the wrong boy.”
He put his face in his hands. I let him.

Down at the water Keola had found something and was holding it up to the light, turning it, a shell or a piece of old glass, and he looked up the beach at us to see if we’d seen. I lifted my hand so he’d know I had. That’s most of being a mother, most days. Lifting your hand so they know you saw. I sat next to this man who had nobody left to lift his hand for, and I didn’t touch him, and I didn’t leave.

After a while I said, quieter, “I’m still angry at you. I want you to know that. Not much. A little. Some nights. I’m angry that you held him and not my mother. I know that doesn’t make sense. She was on the wall. She wouldn’t go in. I’m angry anyway.”
“Okay,” he said into his hands.

“And I’m angry that you came here. Tourists. All of you. I clean your rooms. I’m angry about your pineapple cookie jar, the one you told me about, and your sunset photos and the apartment you rented that used to be somebody’s house. I’m angry that the town has to have you, to live. I’m angry that we need your five dollars on the pillow.”
“Okay.”

“And I’m so grateful to you I could die from it. I’m grateful to you every day. Every single day, when he wakes up, I think: that haole held him. I think it when I look at him. I’ll think it every day of my life.”

He took his hands off his face. He nodded. He didn’t say anything. There wasn’t anything to say. We sat there next to each other on the sand, angry and grateful and sorry, all of it real, none of it canceling anything out, and looked at the water, where my son was standing up to his knees, looking for shells.
“He wants to teach you something,” I said, finally. “He’s been planning it for a month. He told me not to tell you.”
“Teach me what?”
I didn’t answer. I just called down the beach: “Keola! Uncle’s ready!”
And my son turned around in the water, with a shell in each hand, and grinned at us with his big crooked new teeth, and it was the grin from before. From the harbor wall. I hadn’t seen it in a year.
26. Ears In Wes
He took me by the hand, which nobody had done in a year, and he walked me down into the water.

It was warm. That was the first thing. Warm as a bath, the way it had been on the first day, before. Clear as gin over white sand, little yellow fish nosing at my ankles. I stood in it up to my knees and I felt it in the backs of my legs, that old high-board feeling, I can’t see what’s under it, and I stopped.
He felt me stop. He didn’t pull. He just stood there next to me, holding my hand, nine years old, looking up at me.
“It’s okay, Uncle,” he said. “We go slow.”

We went slow. Knees. Thighs. Waist. The water moving round me, lifting a little, setting down, lifting. I hadn’t been in water deeper than a shower in a year. My heart was going like a bird’s. Keola walked next to me with his hand in mine and told me things, chattering, the way kids do when they’re nervous and want you not to be. He told me the yellow fish were called lauʻipala [lah-oo-ee-PAH-lah]. He told me the turtle’s name was honu [HOH-noo]. He told me kai [KYE] means the sea. I stopped walking for a second when he said that, and he waited. He told me his Tūtū used to bring him to the harbor when he was two and hold him in the water by the boat ramp.
When the water was up to my chest he stopped.
“Okay,” he said. “Now you float.”
I laughed. It came out wrong. “Keola, I know how to float. I teach floating. I’ve taught a thousand kids to float.”
“I know,” he said. “But you forgot.”
I want to tell you about the next minute, and I want to tell it simply.
He stood next to me and put one small hand flat under the middle of my back. Exactly where I put mine, for a kid. Exactly where I’d put mine, all that night, under his.
“Lie back, Uncle,” he said. “Arms out. Chin up. Ears in.”
I lay back.
“Give it your weight,” he said. “All of it. Tūtū said give the water your weight, it gives it back. Tūtū said the water knows you by name.”
My words. Her words. The same words, from two ends of the world.
I gave it my weight.

I don’t know how to tell you what that was like, after a year. It was like putting down a suitcase you’ve carried so long you’ve forgotten it’s in your hand. The water came up round my ears and closed over them, and the world went away. The beach, the voices, the wind, the sound of my own breathing, all of it went far off and soft, and there was only the inside sound of the sea, the click and hiss and hum of it, the sound I’d loved my whole life, the sound of being held. Above me the sky was huge and blue and coming down to meet me. The small hand under my back was steady.
And then it wasn’t there.

He’d taken it away. Slowly, the way I take mine away, so gently a kid doesn’t know when it happens. And I was floating. On my own. My arms out, my face to the sky, the sea holding me up as if I weighed nothing, as if I weighed exactly as much as I should.

I knew the trick. I’ve done it to a thousand children. I knew exactly what he was doing, and I let him do it to me anyway, the way you let a child pay for lunch with the money you gave him. And the sea did what it does. It took the weight his hand had been holding and held it instead, all of it, without making anything of it, and gave it back to me as lift.
And then, under the water, in my ears, I heard something.
I’ll tell you what I heard, and you’ll think what you think.
I heard, very far off, the way you hear a radio playing in a house down the street, a woman singing. Slow. Old words. Up and down, like the waves. A voice used to carrying.
And under it, closer, very soft, so soft I could hardly be sure, a voice I knew. A boy’s voice. Counting.
One. Two. Three. Here it comes. Hold.
My own count. In his voice. Calm. Not afraid. Not afraid at all. Counting the waves, the way I’d counted them all that night for both boys, out loud, so they could hear me.
Four. Five. Breathe.

I lay on the water with my ears under and my eyes full and I didn’t move, because I knew that if I moved it would stop. I let it go on. I let the water hold me up, and I listened, and I didn’t count anything. For the first time in a year, I let someone else do the counting.

I don’t know how long. When I came up, Keola was standing a few feet away, up to his chest, watching me, the way he must have watched me that night, from the strap of my bag. Keeping an eye on me. His mother was on the beach, standing at the water’s edge with her arms folded, crying, and pretending not to.
“See?” Keola said. “You remember.”
“Yeah,” I said. “I remember.”
“Tūtū said it knows you by name.”
“I know,” I said. “I heard.”
Said to You
I’ve been talking to you all night. You know that now.
Not to them. Not to the people on the shore, or the man from Ohio, or the woman who cleans the rooms. Not to the boy with the new crooked teeth. To you.

You came down to me a little after the dark came. You remember. The car went up on the street, and the wave came in at the same moment, and your father’s arms opened, and you went under. You went under with your eyes shut and your mouth shut tight, and you couldn’t tell which way was up, and you kicked, and you came up in the smoke, and you couldn’t see anything. Not the wall. Not your father. Not the other boy. Only red dark, and smoke, and me. Deep me. No floor.

You called for your father. Dad. Dad. He was very close. He was calling for you too. You couldn’t hear each other over me, over the wind and the fire and the people. I’m sorry. I’m sorry for that most of all, out of everything. You were so close.
And then the next wave came, and you went down again, and this time you didn’t come up.
I want you to know what happened then, because you were frightened, and I don’t want you to be frightened anymore.

You were afraid of me all your life. You told your father once that you couldn’t see what was under me. That’s what you were most afraid of: the not seeing. The place where the floor goes away. And then there you were, in the place where the floor goes away, in the dark, the thing you were most afraid of in the world.
So I held you.

I’m not good at gentleness. I told you that at the start. But I was gentle with you. I held you the way your father holds a child in the water, flat, with one hand under the small of the back, so you could feel that something had you. I held you so you wouldn’t hit the rocks. I held you so the waves wouldn’t throw you. And I talked to you. I’ve been talking to you ever since. I told you where you were. I told you about the reef and the islands and the rain. I told you about the streams that used to run through this town and the king on his island in the pond. I told you how I lost my floor too, how they turned me away from my own town. I told you what they’ll do up there, after. I told you everything I know, the way you’d tell a child a story in the dark so he’ll stop being afraid of it. The old woman on the hill told her grandson stories every night. I learned it from her.
And then your mother came.

You didn’t know that. Your father didn’t know it either, not then. When the car went up and the wave took you, it tore your father’s bag on the rocks. And she came out. All of her that was left. Fine and pale and soft as flour, she came out into me and spread out through the water all around the wall, all around you, and I carried her to you. I wrapped you in her. She was all around you, in the dark, in the warm. She was right there. She’d wanted to come into the sea at Lahaina, from a boat, in the channel, where the whales sing, and instead she came in at the bottom of a wall in a burning town, at the very same moment as her son. I don’t think she minded. I think that’s where she’d have chosen, if she’d known. Next to you.
So you weren’t alone. You were never alone. Not for one second of it.
And then the singing came down.

The old woman on the wall, the one who’d given her grandson to your father, sat up there above you with her feet hanging over me, and she began to sing. She was singing down into the water, to her boy. She couldn’t see him. She didn’t know which boy was where. Nobody did. So she sang down into me to whoever was there, and I carried it, every word, down to where you were, and you heard it. A song about this place. About shade and water and rain in the night. You didn’t know the words. You didn’t need them.
And somewhere in the middle of it, in the middle of the song, with your mother all around you and the old woman’s voice coming down through the water, you stopped being afraid.
I felt it. You went soft. Your arms opened. You lay back in me, and put your ears in, and gave me your weight.
You floated.

Your father always wanted to see that. He tried for two years. He brought you all the way across the world to see it. He saw the other boy do it, up near the wall, in the smoke, and he cried and said your mother’s name and said, look, he’s floating. He was wrong about which boy. He wasn’t wrong about the floating. You both did. One near the wall in a stranger’s arms. One out here with me. Both of you, that same night, in the same water, for the first time, not afraid.
That was a year ago, they say up there. Up there they count everything. For me it’s still that night. For me it’s always that night. Water doesn’t keep time. It keeps everything else.

Your father came back today. You know that. You were there. He lay down on me with his ears under, the first time in a year, with the other boy’s hand under his back and then not, and he gave me his weight, all of it, the whole year of it. I gave it back. That’s all I’ve ever been able to do. Hold things up. Give back what’s given. Bring things home.

He heard you. I let him. Just for a minute. Just your voice, counting, the way he taught you. He’ll never know if it was real. That’s all right. He doesn’t need to know. He only needs to have heard it.

I won’t give you back to him. I’m sorry. I can’t. Nothing that comes all the way down to me goes back up the old way. But I’ll tell you what I’ve told every child of this town for a thousand years, and what the old woman told her grandson every night, on the hill, in the house that isn’t there:
Everything that comes down to me, I keep. Every drop. Every tear. Every boy. Nothing is lost here. Only mixed.

Your mother’s here. The old woman’s song is here. The streams that used to run through the town are here, the water from the king’s pond, the rain that fell on this island the day it rose. All of it. All of you. In the warm. In the deep part. Where you can’t see what’s under it, because there’s nothing under it now but me.
Lie still. You’re all right.
I’ve got you. I’ve got you both.
